speechtext: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER A WORKABLE SCHEME FOR THE PRAIRIE * PROVINCES

That, in the opinion of this house, a special select committee be appointed to investigate and report on the possibilities of endorsing a workable scheme of crop insurance for the three prairie provinces, such scheme to become operative for the 1940 crop season.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Before the hon. member proceeds with his motion it is my duty to direct the attention of the house to the scope of the resolution. I do not know what the hon. member wishes to discuss with reference to the motion, but last week there was a debate in which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) discussed all matters pertaining to the wheat situation. A declara-

tion of policy was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The rule with reference to questions of this sort is to be found in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, citation 304, and also in May, thirteenth edition. I quote from May, page 316:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members to prevent them from reviving a debate already concluded; and there would be little use in preventing the same question or bill from being offered twice in the same session, if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Before you give your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that crop insurance has been discussed at any time during the present session. We have been discussing the price of wheat and a number of other matters involved, but the question of crop insurance is entirely new.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I was afraid that the debate might take on a wider scope and that we might have a repetition of what had been said before.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think it would be well to hold them down to crop insurance.

During the past ten years agriculture in the western provinces has suffered very severely from drought and from crop failures. These failures were due principally to drought, rust, grasshoppers and other handicaps; in fact, everything that could happen to crops has taken place in those three western provinces. The question might very properly be asked, why do you not include all crops? I can easily understand that, and I do not intend that crop insurance should apply to any province or section that does not wish to have it. I have been asked, however, by the United Farmers of Manitoba in the constituency which I represent, to bring this resolution before the house, and accordingly I do so.
Naturally we in the west talk a good deal about our wheat, wheat prices and crop failures. Wheat occupies a very important place in the agricultural life of this country. It was perhaps news to many who attended the western wheat conference in Winnipeg last December that there were 58,000,000 acres of land under cultivation in Canada, of which 40,000,000 acres are in the three western provinces. That shows the importance of crop insurance as far as western Canada is concerned.
I should like to give a few more figures to illustrate the importance of wheat growing in the west in the economic set-up of this country. It has been stated from reliable

Crop Insurance-Mr. McDonald (Souris)
sources-it was so stated at that conference- that the revenues of the western provinces during those years dropped by over $2,500,000,000. Hon. members can easily understand the impossible position in which western farmers are placed by severe crop losses accompanied by the lowest farm prices ever known. In 1929 the farmers of those three western provinces were able to buy $384,000,000 worth of goods, but by 1933 they were able to buy only $80,000,000 worth. Surely the effects of that decline were felt all over the country. Ontario and Quebec would certainly know that there was something wrong in the west.
We could paint a very dark picture of conditions in western Canada; in fact it would be only honest to say that some of us were beginning to despair of conditions in those provinces; we felt that we had grown wheat and other grain in that part of the country so long that the time had come that we could no longer do so. But that is not true. We had produced 540,000,000 bushels in one year; in another year the crop dropped to 169,000,000 bushels, and we had almost come to believe that western Canada had seen its best days. But last year we grew over 350,000,000 bushels. As one who has gone through the depression and seen Manitoba and the west at its worst as well as at its best. I am sure that with the rehabilitation scheme which this government is carrying on there this country will yet produce great crops of grain. Some sessions ago I heard the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett tell this house that in the growing of wheat wealth can be produced much more rapidly than by any other industry, not excepting gold mining.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he not intend crop insurance to apply to other grains as well as wheat?

I mention
wheat because it is the principal product of the west, and because in the little study I have made of crop insurance it was advised that we should first take one particular commodity. In the west it would be wheat; in the east it might be tobacco or corn or some other commodity. I should have made that explanation earlier. This resolution could apply to any crop, any farm product to which any section of the country might desire to apply it.
Farmers in the west during this depression have received much advice from every section of this country-from bankers, railway-men, manufacturers; and there is nothing . wrong about that, because the subject is
important enough to deserve the most serious consideration. Anything that affects the income of more than half the population of Canada certainly deserves the serious consideration of this house. We believe the time has come to try to safeguard or stabilize in some measure the revenue of the farmers. It is good business for this house and the country to study any possible method of improving conditions on the farm. With my hon. friends who champion the cause of industry I have no quarrel whatever. We have splendid industries in this country, but what good will it do to build up the finest industrial machine if back in the country the great masses of the people are not able to buy manufactured goods? There is at present very little buying power in the place where it should be. There never was such a potential market as there is now in this country if the people only had the buying power.
I am not going to introduce the money question; I do not think it belongs here, although it could very well form part of this discussion. There are two sides to the question: there is that of trying to safeguard the production, and that of doing something to stabilize prices. To-day in parts of western Canada capable farmers know that even if they sow good seed in well cultivated land there is no assurance of a crop, and if they get a good crop they are not sure of the price. That is the impossible position in which the western farmer is placed. What are we going to do about it?	'
It may be asked, why does the farmer not move out? Well, it cannot be done; people have built their homes there. Settlement in the west was encouraged; for many years it was the settled policy of this country to open up the west. The gates were thrown open and great numbers of people were encouraged to go to western Canada. During the war we urged those people by every means to produce, produce, produce, as a patriotic duty. They did so. Western Canada produces the finest wheat in the world, as well as other grains and farm products.
If we are going to discuss wheat at greater length when the Minister of Agriculture 'brings down his bill I shall not take the time of the house now to speak further of the value and importance of wheat growing in this country. But I should like to give a few figures relating to Saskatchewan. Comparing the years 1929 and 1933, the decline in farm production was only six per cent, but the decrease in prices was 63 per cent. For purposes of comparison let us take other commodities closely allied with the buying needs of the farmer. For example, the decline in the price of farm
1572	COMMONS
Crop Insurance-Mr. McDonald (Souris)
implements was only 16 per cent, but production dropped 80 per cent. In cement the volume of production dropped 80 per cent, but the price dropped only 18 per cent. Iron and steel prices dropped only 20 per cent but volume of production decreased 83 per cent. Is it fair, is it honest, that the farmers of this country should be compelled (to go on producing with a decline of 63 per cent in the price of their product, when the manufacturer of farm implements takes a reduction of only 16 per cent, iron and steel 20 per cent, and cement 18 per cent? Of course I know that in respect of some other commodities the decrease in price was greater.
Let us look at some of the conditions applicable to good crop insurance. The people of Manitoba are studying crop insurance at the present time. Saskatchewan has given considerable study to the question; the United States has made an extensive study of it, and we in this house must do likewise in view of what the Minister of Agriculture has announced, because I feel certain that the government intends to bring in something in the nature of crop insurance, we hope at this session.
We should not continue the present policy, because it has placed the farmers of the west in such a position that they see very little hope for the future. The effect of the paralysis of the purchasing power of the west will be felt in every part of the country; it cannot be confined to the west alone, any more than a disease which may attack one part of the body can be confined to that part only. For that reason we should do what we can to correct this situation. I believe we should look into the feasibility of crop insurance in an endeavour to safeguard the farmer as far as possible against factors which are beyond his control. Certainly the farmer cannot control the weather, which has so much to do with the production of crops. Certainly he has very little to say about the fiscal policies of any country other than his own, in order that he may maintain a decent standard of living through the sale of the goods he has produced. Industry has been able to safeguard itself by insurance. We have all kinds of insurance-life, automobile and hail insurance-and by the way that is the only crop insurance we have ever had in the west; any other crop insurance plan ever tried has failed because we have not had sufficient information to give the insurance companies a proper basis on which they could fix the cost of such insurance.
As I mentioned a moment ago, industry is able to protect itself through insurance, and the farmer will have to do the same thing if (Mr. G. W. McDonald.]
he is to survive. It is expected that some time in the future this government will introduce a system of unemployment insurance, which I feel reasonably sure will not apply to the fanner, if we are to judge from the legislation that was introduced by the previous government. For that reason the farmer has every right to ask for crop insurance in order that he may receive the protection that industry will receive by way of unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation and other insurance plans that have been devised to safeguard industry and the workers in industry.
In the beginning we should have the simplest possible crop insurance plan, because that is the only way we can gain practical experience; and I think that insurance should apply to some principal crop. We cannot have it apply to every crop; we must take the most important one, wheat. The contracts should be very clear and simple, and should not be open to dispute. In addition, no form of crop insurance should encourage poor farming. We have no right to introduce into this house a bill that will have the effect of making the farmer look more to his crop insurance than to better methods of farming. We must avoid that very real danger. The amount of insurance should be arrived at scientifically; we should have all the information as to the type of soil, what it has produced in the past, what kind of farmer the man is, and all the rest of the data necessary to show the physical value of each farm, and we should not insure to the extent of more than seventy-five per cent of that amount.
Then there is the question of the collection of premiums. From the resolution I have introduced it might be surmised that we wanted the government to do this free for the three western provinces. That is not the idea of crop insurance, though in view of the present position of the western fanner the government at first would have to do that. We have many farmers in the west who would be pleased to pay their own premiums, if they could once get started; but in instituting such a scheme I suggest that the government take at least a portion of the premiums, if not all, in the form of w'heat or some other farm product, particularly in a year when there was a large crop. That would have the effect of taking a large part of the surplus off the market, and would help stabilize prices. It would have a double benefit; it would help the farmers finance themselves and would help the government put the farmers in the position of being able to pay their own premiums. After all, any industry that is worth while should stand on its own feet.

National Health-Mr. Mclvor
I have touched only a few of the principal features of crop insurance. There is one other point I should like to mention, however, and it is this. In years when we have large crops, such as we had this year in many parts of western Canada, the municipalities could do a great deal to help themselves if they would build municipal elevators in which part of the jrop could be stored. Why do I advocate a scheme of that kind? I do so because every year we have had a crop failure the farmers have had to come and ask this government to provide seed and feed, and in almost every case when the farmer came to pay back the advance it has taken three bushels of wheat in the fall to pay for one bushel of seed obtained in the spring. That being so, I believe something should be done by way of storing grain, not in commercial elevators, so that it may be available in time of need. The cost of providing feed, seed and direct relief in western Canada has brought bankruptcy to most of the municipalities, placed a heavy burden on the provinces as a result of which they are unable to finance themselves without the help of this government, and placed a heavy strain upon the finances of the federal authorities. At the conference held in Winnipeg last December it was stated that $900,000.000 had been spent on relief. We cannot continue under present conditions, and it is for that reason I now bring the subject matter of this motion to the attention of the government.

PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government of Canada should try to secure amendments to the British North America Act, to provide periodical health examinations and provision for suitable treatment for all those suffering from disease.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the resolution
appears in its present form so that it may not be called by a false name and debated under some other head. We realize that as a dominion government we cannot go ahead without the cooperation of the provinces. Therefore we want to tell them, in the words of Dickens, that "Barkis is willin'."
I bring the resolution before the house, first, for the sake of the doctors, and, second, on behalf of the sick. I speak not from hearsay but from personal information and from what I have seen in Saskatchewan, Manitoba
and around the head of the lakes. The worthy hon. member who has seconded this motion (Mr. Howden) used to take me out under his wing, especially on a Sunday night when he had a few calls to make, and in that way I was permitted to see and to understand for myself. I saw both sides of the case. I can see that doctor, on my advice and invitation, visiting the home of a man, the father of five children, who could not pay five cents to the doctor. The father was suffering from a severe foot infection, and as a result part of it had to be cut away. I can still see that man sitting with his foot in a pail of hot water. I can still see that worthy doctor taking the foot from the water, and handling it as if it were a tender baby. Who would pay him? I say that sort of thing is not fair. It has been said of that doctor that at one time the community in which he lived owed him $75,000, and, if I may be permitted to use the doctor's own plain language, he would not "get a blamed cent of it." No doctor whose services may be worth $50 to $70 a day should have to give them free of charge. We have great wealth in Canada and, as I said on another occasion, there ought to be enough for everybody. But there is not sufficient for all, because of the greed of some. Selfishness is perhaps one of the greatest causes of much of our suffering.
I can remember an occasion in northern Manitoba when a young doctor took me with him on a forty-mile drive. Taking his kit, he expected to perform some surgical work. When we arrived at our destination conditions were not very comfortable for him and were especially uncomfortable for the patient. However, working under difficult conditions, the doctor did the best he could, and the operation proved successful. Following his work we drove home, shooting some wild ducks and having our lunch on the way. I was present at an interview between that doctor and the farmer. The doctor's fee, to cover a forty mile trip and a surgical operation, was $17.50. When he was informed of the amount, the farmer objected. Then, as one might expect the doctor sat back and permitted the sky pilot to do the talking. I informed that man that for the type of operation which had been performed the doctor should receive $150. I said to him; "The doctor will not take a cent for his services because you have not appreciated what he has done in saving the life of your wife. Perhaps you think your wife was not worth very much." Some time after that however the man had a good crop and was able to make a payment.
National Health-Mr. Mclvor

I am sure there are medical men in the house who come from centres where during the depression-and the same may apply even now-they received very little for their services. That would be true especially in relief cases. I could take hon. members to a home in Fort William where a doctor had been called to attend a sick child. As it was not expected to live, I, too, had heen called. As one might expect, the minister beat the doctor to it. I can still see that doctor-and I do not mind giving his name; it was Doctor McCartney, a very fine type of returned soldier-attending that child as if it were the most valuable thing on earth. Yet he could not get five cents for his work. I say, therefore, that the resolution is worthy of support, first, for the sake of the doctors.
May I point out, too, that it should be supported for the sake of the sick. I heard of a farmer in O'Connor district, near Fort William, who refused to go to the hospital for treatment because he did not expect to live much longer anyway, and did not wish to leave his family in debt. Undoubtedly he should have had treatment.
To my mind the two reasons I have submitted are sufficient to warrant the support of the resolution. I know the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) will give it his fatherly approval just as soon as the means are at his disposal. Prevention is the best kind of cure. Our doctors tell us that if patients could be treated in the early stages, the cost of illness would not be so great. We know however that the surgeon or doctor is called in only as a last resort, and that in many cases surgical operations are performed when it may be too late. The people hardest hit in this way are the greatest producers of wealth, namely the toilers, and especially the farmers. In some communities great difficulty is experienced in getting a doctor. For some time in a district east of Port Arthur the people have been trying to obtain the services of a doctor. They would pay part of the expense, and would find some other way to provide the rest of his salary, but so far however they have not been able to secure the services of a medical man. Under present circumstances medical attention costs them far more than it shopld.
I do not want to take much time in a discussion of this motion, because we want to hear from members in different parts of the house. I would say that one of the outstanding needs of our time is that of health examination, especially for those who are contemplating marriage. I believe the absence of such examination is one of the greatest

causes of divorce. The doctors know more about that than I do, and they will be able to speak with authority.
I leave the matter now for the consideration of the house, because to my mind health examinations and treatment for those suffering from disease represent one of the outstanding needs of our time. From Cape Breton on the east to Vancouver on the west, and extending up into the northern country, periodical health examination and proper medical treatment are very necessary. I know it is difficult to get the money, but under present circumstances it is costing the country far more than it otherwise would.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the session of 1931 it was my privilege and pleasure to bring before the house the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
It will 'be seen that I asked only for a measure of state medicine. Thirteen hon. members took part in the debate on that resolution, and, with the exception of two, I am happy to say that they were all favourably disposed. In fact one member on the government side, since deceased, sent me over a note asking me not to withdraw the resolution but to allow it to go to a vote. However, the leader of the government took exception to the resolution and set his face quite definitely against it. He indicated that if the resolution were accepted by the government it would mean that the government would be obliged to bring in state medicine in some form, and that the resolution, in the terms in which it then appeared, meant practically the sweeping away of all existing medical services in the country. In the following year I moved another resolution in the following language:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration steps which would:	(a) provide for
periodic medical examination of the Canadian people; (b) afford medical relief for those suffering from disease.
This resolution was substantially the same as the one moved to-day by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). Under the circumstances it is not difficult for me to come to his assistance and support his contention by seconding his motion.
It is not my intention to spend a great deal of time in a discussion of the resolution; it speaks plainly enough for itself. It asks that the government secure authority to provide for periodical health examinations and to afford relief to those suffering from disease.

National Health-Mr. Howden
I would proceed first by asking the house: Is it desirable that we should have periodical medical examinations? We are told that thousands of people, in fact hundreds of thousands of people in this country die yearly from preventable diseases. We are told that between three and four per cent of the population of Canada are constantly sick and under medical care, and that medical services cost the people in the vicinity of 1300,000,000 yearly.
What would be the advantage of periodical medical examinations? Speaking generally,
I say that periodical medical examinations would discover, in the case of children, bad *teeth, diseased tonsils, defective hearing and eyesight, scrofula, chorea, tuberculosis, and many other forms of disease which would have disastrous results in a short time or lead to more serious trouble later. Then in the case of adults, periodical examinations would discover tuberculosis, heart disease, the greatest destroyer of human life; hyperarterial tension, and many other conditions. So far as children are concerned, if these conditions are discovered in time, about ninety-five per cent of all cases can be corrected. The child may then go on in its healthful way, strong, intelligent, and rejoicing, whereas if the condition is not discovered in time, we may have a feeble youngster who has difficulty in fighting life's battles.
As far as adults are concerned, I think we are all indirectly familiar with the conditions which I have mentioned and realize that periodical medical examinations would be of decided benefit. This whole matter was summed up quite well in a pamphlet put out some years ago by the health league of Canada. It started off 'by stating what I have said, that many thousands of people die from diseases that could be prevented. It then goes on:
There is one solution. Periodic health examination-a periodic and thorough overhauling by a competent physician. To induce people to adopt this solution is a task demanding prompt and constant attention of health authorities, thoughtful citizens, and statesmen.
Disease strikes from coast to coast. It is a national menace and combating it a national problem. Dominion leadership is needed, because at present there is no uniformity of health management. In some places health is well safeguarded, in others, deplorably neglected. Cooperation between the dominion and the provinces in a concerted attack upon venereal disease has proven the value of maintaining a united front against disease. Not until this unity is achieved in attacking all diseases, can we expect a rapid change in the present unsatisfactory disease and mortality rates.
This deals at least in a brief and inefficient way with the first part of the resolution. Surely no one who considers the matter seri- [DOT] 71492-100
ously can help but realize the benefit of health examinations, at least once a year or, even better, twice yearly. The people of all countries, particularly the people of the United States, are becoming more alive to the need of state help in the matter of health relief. In 1935 the United States government passed the social security act. I am not familiar with its provisions, but I understand it is a measure which affords relief in many forms to the people of that country. I believe it provides relief for the unemployed, relief by way of public and health services, relief to expectant mothers, child relief, and so on. The President of the United States, realizing that many of the services provided by this act as emergency measures would become permanent once the act had been put into force, created a so-called interdepartmental committee and instructed it to coordinate the health and welfare activities. The chairman of the committee is Miss Josephine Roche, formerly assistant secretary of the treasury; the other members are the undersecretary for agriculture, the assistant secretaries of interior and labour, and the chairman of the social security board.
The social security board, in assuming its duties, asked the technical committee on medical care to investigate health and welfare conditions in the United States. The technical committee on medical care made an intensive study of health activities and summarized its findings in a report which was presented to the interdepartmental committee, which in turn passed it on to the president. The president recognized the urgency of the needs described in the report and suggested that the interdepartmental committee' lay the technical committee's report before a public health conference. As a result, a national health conference was called, which assembled at Washington in July, 1938.
Five recommendations were laid before the health conference at that time. I believe those five recommendations are well worthy of the consideration of hon. members of this house, and with your permission, sir, I am going to quote some of them.
The first recommendation was that the existing federal-state cooperative program for general public health services and for maternal and child health services be further extended through enlarged grants in aid to the states. Under this recommendation the committee first proposed an expansion of general public health services. Prevention must always be regarded as the first step in health programs. The expansion of the preventive health service means the strengthening and expansion of organized public health services which are



National Health-Mr. Howden
furnished primarily in the states and in local communities. Federal participation should be increased with a view to equalizing the public health services throughout the nation by strengthening such services where they are weak.
The committee further proposed that there be increased federal participation in public health services particularly in promoting an attack on certain important causes of sickness and death, for the control of which we already have effective weapons. I do not know that I need dilate on these various forms of sickness. Although they are not specifically stated, they are definitely hinted at. Certainly tuberculosis is one of them, and transcending even tuberculosis in importance I think is venereal disease, particularly syphilis. Members of this house are probably aware that last year the United States congress passed a bill providing for a federal expenditure of $5,000,000 the first year and $7,000,000 the second year, and such further sums as might be required for the balance of a ten-year period, for the purpose of fighting venereal disease alone.
The committee's recommendation calls for a careful but steady expansion towards a ten-year goal, when an adequate program of expanded public health services would require additional expenditures by federal, state and local governments of about S200,000,000 a year, or about $1.50 per capita. So that the first part of the first recommendation of the national health committee involved in expansion of public health services alone the sum of $200,000,000 a year.
The second part of the first recommendation deals with the expansion of special maternal and child health services. The committee proposed an expansion of the federal-state cooperative program already developed under the social security act. The goal is to assure to the mothers and children of all income groups and in all parts of the United States at least the minimum medical services which are essential to a reduction of the needlessly high maternal mortality rates and death rates among newborn infants, and to prevent diseases and conditions which occur in childhood and lead to serious disabilities in later life. If all of this were undertaken the program would require by the tenth year a total additional expenditure of about $165,000,000 a year. That is to say the first recommendation entailed an expenditure by the United States of $365,000,000 a year for public welfare and maternal and child welfare.
The second recommendation was this-and my reason, Mr. Speaker, for discussing this 
program in some detail is that it is such a comprehensive program of national health; if by any far-off chance we could embrace such a program in this country, we should indeed be considered a very fortunate people. The second recommendation was concerned with federal grants in aid for the construction of needed hospitals, and for the provision of temporary maintenance grants in the first three years after these new hospitals are built, in order to assist the local communities in taking over the responsibility for using and supporting them. The committee's studies show that the states need about 360,000 additional beds-taking into account beds needed in general, tuberculosis and mental disease hospitals, in both rural and urban areas, and that they need at least 500 health and diagnostic centres-no doubt comparable to our district health units in Canada [DOT]-in areas not readily accessible to hospitals or not sufficiently populated to require or to be able to support fully equipped hospitals. Improvement and modernization of existing facilities is, of course, included. Averaged over a ten-year period, the total annual cost of this program, including both construction and temporary maintenance, is estimated at a little under $150,000,000.
The third recommendation calls for federal grants in aid to the states to help them meet the costs of a medical care program, and this is the one I wish particularly to emphasize. It is a medical care program for recipients of relief or public assistance and other persons with low incomes who are able to meet the ordinary costs of living but not the extraordinary costs of illness. That to me, Mr. Speaker, is the hub of the whole thing. I believe that about sixty per cent of our population in Canada receive incomes of less than $1,000 a year. While I do not wish to rehash what has been said before, it must be evident to every lion, member that the family man who is not earning more than $1,000 a year will need to use every cent of his income to provide for his family and himself, and naturally he does not put away any money for sickness. When sickness comes it is a burden which he is little able to face, and if he is an honest man and insists upon paying his way, it certainly leaves him in a sad financial condition for a long time to come.
The facts brought to the attention of the committee show that the one-third of the population which is in the lower income brackets is receiving inadequate medical service in the United States. I think the same holds here. This applies to more than 20,000,000 persons who are supported by general relief, work relief, old age assistance and

National Health-Mr. Howden
other forms of public aid, and to about 20,000,000 other persons and families with incomes of S800 a year or less. These 40,000,000 are doubly handicapped. They have higher rates of sickness and disablement than prevail among groups with larger incomes, and they have less capacity to buy and pay for the services they need. Current provisions for medical services are inadequate to meet their needs. The committee recommended that the federal government assist the states from grants in aid to strengthen medical services for these two particular groups of the population.
The fourth recommendation, presented as complementary to the third, called for grants in aid to states to enable them to set up a general program of medical care, either by the use of taxation or by state health insurance programs, or by a combination of the two.
The first three recommendations took account of general or special preventive services, hospital construction and modernization and services for the medically needy. The fourth recommendation turns to the problems of persons who are ordinarily self-supporting. The committee directed attention to the economic burdens created by sickness, especially among low income groups, and concluded that there is need for measures which will enable people to anticipate and to meet sickness costs on a budget basis.
Without great increase in total national expenditure, the burdens of sickness costs on families and on the public can be greatly reduced through arrangements to distribute these costs among groups of people and over periods of time. The more adequate prevention and care thus made possible would lessen both individual disasters and the public burdens arising from dependency.
The committee recommended consideration of a comprehensive program designed to increase and improve medical services for the entire population. To finance the program, two sources of funds could be drawn upon: general taxation or special tax assessments, and specific insurance contributions from the potential beneficiaries of an insurance system. The committee recommended consideration of both methods, recognizing that they may be used separately or in combination.
Though this fourth recommendation deals primarily with medical care for self-sustaining persons, the committee recognized that it would be unsound for the states to develop for the self-supporting population medical care programs which are separate and apart from whatever the states might develop for needy persons. Accordingly, the committee 71492-100J
proposed that while the fourth recommendation deals primarily with state medical programs for self-supporting persons, a sound state plan should make provision for the care of the needy persons under the same system that is developed for the self-supporting.
I think the fifth and last recommendation is also worthy of notice. The fifth recommendation proposed that federal action be taken toward the development of disability compensation-that is, benefit payments to insured workers who are temporarily or permanently disabled. This recommendation contemplates insurance against loss of wages on account of disability.
Under the present social security program, millions of workers may count on some continuance of partial income in lieu of their regular wTages when they become unemployed and are able to work. Under the workmen's compensation laws, most of them are protected against wage loss resulting from accident or injury arising out of employment. But generally they have no protection against wage loss resulting from non-industrial sickness or accident. A limited number of workers do have some such protection through voluntary insurance schemes, commercial or non-profit, but they are a small minority in the total.
There is good reason to believe that insurance against disability can best be treated not by a single insurance system but by two systems closely coordinated. There is, first, the problem of the temporarily disabled worker-the worker who has an acute illness and for whom there is every reason to expect that, after a few weeks or a few months, he will recover and return to work. There is, second, the problem of the permanently disabled worker-the worker who, by reason of crippling or chronic illness, will probably never again be able to enter gainful employment.
Temporary disability compensation, with a substantial waiting period-seven, ten or fourteen days-with benefits calculated at fifty per cent of wages for a benefit period of at least twenty-six weeks, would cost approximately one per cent of wages. The cost should probably be divided between employers and workers, though a share of the cost might be carried by general taxation. Such an insurance system would normally be financed on an annual fiscal basis, involving no reserves other than for operating and contingency purposes.
Permanent disability insurance, with benefits geared to old age and survivor's benefits, would probably cost two-tenths to three-tenths of one per cent of wages in the earlier
National Health-Mr. Howden

years, 'but as time went on the cost might be expected to rise, depending on the extent of the benefits provided and numerous other factors. This type of insurance could be established by liberalizing the present federal old age pension system.
There we have a comprehensive system of national health insurance. It provides for an extension of public health services and maternal and child welfare work; the building of needed hospitals, the institution of district health units in various parts of the country; health service for those on relief and families which cannot afford to pay for it. It offers a form of health insurance to families which would have great difficulty in meeting the cost of large and extended medical services. Lastly it provides protection for workers who are unemployed, and for people who through chronic illness, crippling or old age will be permanently unemployable. It is an important, comprehensive and complete system of health insurance. It has been submitted by the President of the United States to the various states and organizations throughout the states. It has in fact been the subject of heated and vitriolic debate in that country. But there can be no question in the mind of any sane and honest individual who has the welfare of his country and his fellow citizens at heart that the adoption of a program of this kind would be eminently desirable and to the advantage of us all.
Inasmuch as the motion of the hon. member for Fort William practically requires state health insurance-for it is useless to provide for periodical health examinations if relief is not provided where sickness is found to exist-it is not necessary to abolish the health service we have at the present time. We have an excellent health service, extensive hospitals, and a sound and efficient practice of medicine. A large majority of the medical practitioners are philanthropically inclined; they are serious and able. We have health units pretty well spread over the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and finding their way through Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Health and medical services are provided by many fraternal societies; the Kiwanis and other service clubs are doing an excellent work in supplying needed measures of medical relief. Sickness and life insurance companies provide a measure of nursing service in time of illness. The value of ordinary municipal health service is not to be ignored: school nurses examine the children from time to time and ascertain the nature of the illness that is keeping children at home. School children fortunately have the benefit of more than an examination, because according to

law in most of our provinces the children are required to submit to inoculation against diphtheria and typhoid and scarlet fever, as well as vaccination against smallpox, and any disease from which they may be suffering is attended to immediately in order that they may return to school as soon as possible. The examination of school children therefore is a valuable service to the country, and we may look forward hopefully to the day when diphtheria, typhoid and scarlet fever will practically cease to exist, just as smallpox has been successfully eradicated.
This is all excellent work, but it falls far short of a general scheme of national health. The poor sick are always poor, and very often sick. They get the poorest medical attention, just as they receive the least consideration in other matters. I urge upon the federal government that they take this matter into serious consideration. All we ask is that they interest themselves in the health of the Canadian people beyond merely administering the Food and Drugs Act and looking after leprosy-which by the way I have never seen and never expect to see, and I am sixty years old-and a few other things that make no difference at all to the Canadian people. If this is all that is done, the federal health department might just as well not exist; and if it might just as well not exist, why not do away with it?

speechtext:
I am glad to hear the Minister of Pensions and National Health say " hoar, hear," for I know he is sympathetic to the health movement. I have little doubt that if he were to receive any encouragement from the government to which he belongs we should soon have a desirable system of care of national health.
In conclusion I ask the government to take the same degree of interest in the health of the Canadian people that is being taken by governments not only in the United States and Europe but in South America and Africa and every other country under the face of heaven.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
I agree in general with the purpose of the motion of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) rather than with the method proposed by him for carrying it out. Having been many years ago a medical practitioner, I sympathize with the idea of greater care of the people's health. I realize that the hon. member for Fort William is moved in this matter by his sympathy and kindness of heart. Being a clergyman by profession, he has had much

National Health-Mr. Manion
experience, as all medical practitioners have, in entering the homes of the people and seeing the sickness and sorrow which is the lot particularly of the poor; and he feels that something should be done about it. With that feeling I think all hon. members will be in sympathy. One difficulty is the expense, in these times when governments are hard pressed for money, and another, which is at the present time almost insurmountable, is that of securing the necessary change in the British North America Act.
A good deal has been done towards the protection of the health of the people. I think the insurance companies, not only of Canada but of the United States and other countries, deserve much credit for their splendid work in encouraging their policyholders to undergo annual medical examination. For example, within the last ten days I had a thorough examination at the expense of an insurance company in which I have held a policy for some years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: The result was good?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: Pretty fair; good enough at any rate, I may inform my hon. friend, that I think I shall be hanging around when the next election takes place.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friends are pleased.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: I do not know whether or not the applause is flattering.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Well, I will take a chance on that. Without doubt the insurance companies have carried on this work in the hope that it would pay them to do so, though so far as I know they have been unable to prove as yet that this work has brought them any financial return. Recently, however, I saw some figures which indicated that in 1938 some six thousand people took advantage of the opportunity to get medical examination at the expense of the insurance companies in which they held policies. That is a large number of people. Some of the diseases which may be discovered by these early examinations, even at a time when the patient may seem to be in reasonably good health, are cancer, tuberculosis, diabetes, Bright's disease and heart diseases. There may be others that I have overlooked, but these five came to my mind. If I may give a little free medical advice to the whole house, a complete medical examination at least every year, and I should say every six months, is advisable for all men over fifty years of age. I hope that may make a little
business for the medical profession, incidentally, though it will not be any advantage to me because I am not practising. Regular medical examinations every six months or every year would in many cases arrest the progress of some malady which might carry off a man or a woman if it were not discovered in time. The diseases I have mentioned may be discovered early in their development and, by proper treatment, their progress halted. The great leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the idol of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), when a comparatively young man was discovered to have some defect in his health. I am not certain whether it had to do with his lungs or his heart, but I think he had what was described in those days as a weakness in the lungs. He was advised to take good care of himself. So well did he do that, despite the fact that he was a hard worker all his life, he lived to a ripe old age.^ If I may be forgiven for mentioning it, that is a good illustration of the' advantage of the early discovery of an illness or disease.
So that even if a debate such as this does nothing more than stir up interest in the health of the individual, it accomplishes a great deal. At the same time it should not be forgotten that this whole question of periodical medical examinations is bound up with health insurance, old age pensions, unemployment insurance and other social services which in some countries at least are being progressively entered upon. Even England, which is far fiom being a socialist country, has gone in for social services to a greater degree, I think, than most other countries. Indeed, as I said in this house a few days ago, I think during the debate on unemployment insurance, we in Canada might do well to copy more of England s methods in such matters as social services. Canada is very far behind in all these matters, and we might well do more than we have been doing in caring not only for the health but also for the lives of our people.
The latter part of the resolution deals with state medicine, and I do not know that at the present time I would come out wholeheartedly for that. The last few words of the resolution are as follows:
Provide periodical health examinations and provision for suitable treatment for all those suffering from disease.
That is really state medicine, and at the present time, as far as my information goes, the medical men themselves' are opposed to that proposal. There are individuals, of whom I think the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) is one, judging from his remarks in this house on a number of occasions,
National Health-Mr. Manion

who favour state medicine, but I think the majority of the medical profession do not. To their credit be it said that in the years that have gone the medical profession have always been in the forefront when any proposal was made which would benefit the public.

If I may, Mr. Speaker,
I would inform my hon. friend that the house committee of the American Medical Association have accepted the first three and the fifth of those resolutions, but have discarded the fourth.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for that information. I do not pretend to be up to date in regard to medical questions at the present time, but I think I am correct in saying that a majority of the medical men in Canada at any rate, and I believe in the United States, are not favourable to state medicine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: If my hon. friend would permit me-I will put it in the form of a question,-is it not a fact that at present any province that so desired could embark on state medicine?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Yes; before concluding I
was going to mention that of course this is at the present time a provincial matter.
I was going to say that the medical men themselves have originated all the advances that have been made in regard to public health. All down through the ages the medical men have been taking away from their livelihood by discovering new methods of treatment and giving them to the world. We can look back at practically all the discoveries in medicine, such as anaesthesia, antisepsis, antitoxin in diphtheria, the treatment of syphilis and various other treatments, and with only one exception that comes to my mind these discoveries have been given freely to the world, without any profit to the person who discovered them. There is another discovery that I overlooked for the moment; that is, the discovery of the insulin treatment for diabetes by our own Doctor Banting of Toronto. It is true that Doctor Banting did receive a reward; he was appointed as head of a research institute which is doing splendid work. But men in the medical profession, all down through the ages, have been discovering methods of treating disease and offering them freely to the world. The one exception that comes to my mind, though there may be others, is the discovery of 606 for the treatment of syphilis, which was patented so that the medical profession, and through them the patients, had to pay quite 
high prices for the treatment. It was discovered in Germany, and I do not say that with any desire to criticize the German people. I do sometimes criticize their present leader, but I have no criticism of the German people themselves. One other treatment I could have mentioned, perhaps, is the discovery of vaccination many years ago by a country practitioner in England. All the treatments I have mentioned, with the single exception, were given freely to the public, even though it meant that in giving them the medical profession were taking away part of their own livelihood.
I mention this only because it suggests that the fact that the majority of the medical profession oppose state medicine seems to me proof that this is not quite the proper time to institute such a system.
There is another method growing up in various parts of the world whereby medical men band together and form a sort of clinic. In consideration of receiving so much per month from a number of families, they care for them. There is really nothing very new in that, because I well remember that thirty years ago I was doing the same thing on a fairly large scale at the head of the lakes, the vicinity from which the mover of the resolution (Mr. Mclvor) comes. The scheme was of an industrial type. I was looking after the employees of three or four very large corporations. I remember that one of them at one time had as many as 1,600 men employed. Regularly I made my morning visit to the plant at half past seven, and held my clinic before I began what I regarded as my regular day's work. This system is much the same as that which is being developed to-day. The employees in the plant paid one dollar a month, and in return received medical and surgical attention, drugs, ambulance service, hospitalization, and all that any man would require in respect of any illness.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The ancient Chinese
system.

speechtext:
Yes, to a certain extent it was the ancient Chinese system, the system under which you keep the patient well. He pays you while you are keeping him well, and stops paying when you do not. As a matter of fact I think it is a rather good system. There is this about it, that they pay, whereas to-day a great many who become sick do not pay. From the point of view of the medical men I imagine they would much prefer a system under which all would pay.
One development which has been a great boon to the working man has been the introduction of workmen's compensation

National Health-Mr. Woodsworth
boards. This system was introduced in Ontario I do not know how many years ago- it cannot be very many, because I can well remember that there was no workmen's compensation board in the early days of my practice.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: It was introduced by Sir James Whitney.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Yes. There was no workmen's compensation board in the first ten years of my practice. At that time if a man was injured and wished to secure damages he had to sue the company, and very often if he hoped to win he had to carry his case up through the courts. The companies worked on the principle that if an individual beat them in court they were placed in a disadvantageous position in respect of other accident cases. The operations of the workmen's compensation board have brought great happiness to the working man. It is a system which is now in force I believe in every province in Canada, although some of the provinces adopted it only recently.
As I say, the difficulty involved in the proposal of the hon. member lies in the attempt to change the British North America Act. The very fact that it is necessary to change the British North America Act to put into force a system such as this emphasizes the fact that health is really a provincial matter and not a dominion matter. While I might be very sad if the health branch were wiped out, 'because it is headed by a minister who is one of my very best friends in the house, and while I should not like to see him out of a job-

The
pensions would remain.
