Yes. But I have wondered sometimes if the dominion were not going outside its proper scope in dealing as much as it does with health matters. At the same time I believe it was the party to which I belong which brought the health branch into operation. I remember advocating the appointment of the first deputy minister, Doctor Amyot, and also the present one, Doctor Wodehouse.
I suppose, however, that the hon. member for Fort William does not expect the resolution to carry. I imagine he has accomplished his purpose in drawing the matter to the attention of the house. I have expressed my sympathy with the general idea. I imagine his resolution will receive the sympathy of many other hon. members, including that of
the minister, and probably the hon. member will consider he has done all that he set out to do.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps the form in which the resolution is presented is not very fortunate. However on behalf of our group I should like to associate myself with the principle which seems to underlie it. I would rather take exception to the last words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), that sympathy is about all that we need at this time. As regards a great many of these things I think the government ought to be pressed to take action.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: I did not say sympathy was all you need. I thought sympathy was all you would get.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
That is a somewhat different matter. Recently the Health League of Canada presented an interesting brief to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. I shall take the liberty of quoting a part of the submissions which, it seems to me, summarize the situation:
1.	That the cost of illness in Canada is so great that it imposes a very heavy burden on the community and on the individual.
2.	That the direct cost falls largely on the provinces, municipalities and individuals.
3.	That a very large proportion of illness is preventable.
4.	That the discoveries in the field of preventive medicine are not applied to the task of preventing illness as they should be and that the amount of money spent on preventive measures is inadequate.
5.	That the value of cooperation between the dominion and the provinces has been proven and has proved to be effective in the field of venereal disease control.
6.	That this type of cooperation should be extended to other fields.
7.	That there is nothing in the British North America Act which prevents cooperation and the development of coordinated action throughout the dominion.
I shall not go farther. The last paragraph brings me to the resolution itself, which urges that the British North America Act be amended so that the dominion might more thoroughly enter into this field. I am inclined to think that the Health League of Canada was nearly correct when it pointed out that there is really nothing in the British North America Act which is out of keeping with action along this line. Here again I would read from their brief in support of the contention that "(7) there is nothing in the British North America Act which prevents cooperation and the development of coordinated action throughout the dominion:"
Under section 91 of the British North America Act exclusive legislation of the par-

National Health-Mr. Woodsworth
liament of Canada is extended to all matters coming within classes of subjects listed in this section. Subject No. 11 is quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals.
This is the only reference to health in the British North America Act.
I noticed it was taken for granted by the mover of the resolution that the British North America Act would have to be changed. It would appear that the leader of the opposition assumed the resolution could not be carried out without changes to the constitution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext: Section 92 also refers to the subject.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
I will come to that. I quote the brief:
In section 92 exclusive powers of the provincial legislatures are defined. Subsection 7 assigns to the provinces the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province and other than marine hospitals.
That refers to institutions only.
In view of the fact that in 1867 there were no departments of health and preventive medicine was scarcely thought of, this matter is not definitely taken up in the act.
Section 91 states: "It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the consent of the House of Commons to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces."
In other words, all residuary matters may be dealt with by the dominion.
It would seem that there is no good reason why the dominion should not enter into full participation in any scheme for the promotion of health throughout Canada.
That seems to be a not unreasonable argument. I shall not go into the constitutional question at any length, but I think we have taken some of these matters altogether too much for granted. We have failed to recognize the developments which have taken place in more recent years.
As to the position of our own group, let me say that from the very inception of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation we have emphasized the necessity of socialized health services. One of the planks in our platform is that there should be cooperation with the provinces in creating dominion-wide socialized health services. A pamphlet recently issued by the national council of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation explains this as follows:
The dominion and the provinces have their ministers and departments of health. In the main, however, health services are a matter of private arrangement with the medical profession, though there are important exceptions.

Several provinces already have some municipal doctors, free tuberculosis sanatoria and cancer and other clinics. But these hardly touch the problem, let alone solve it. On the whole, adequate medical care is still a luxury for the majority of our men, women and children. In thousands of cases serious illness and even death could be avoided if the patients had proper medical attention in time. But most workers, farmers and fishermen can only afford to go to the doctor or even hospital when they become convinced that they can no longer delay with safety. The result is unnecessary and preventable suffering and loss of life.
In this respect, too, Canada is behind most countries. Some form of state medicine is already operating in many lands such as Great Britain, the Scandinavian countries and New Zealand. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation urges the institution of socialized health services for all Canadian citizens and will endeavour to coordinate the work in the provinces on a dominion-wide scale.
That is what we propose and what we are bound to advocate on every suitable occasion. It seems to me that this resolution hardly goes far enough. It asks for periodical health examination and for the suitable treatment of all those suffering from disease. There is nothing specific in that. It is something which cannot be done effectively except by some form of state medicine. Sooner or later we shall have to come to that. The leader of the opposition, himself a medical man, suggests that a considerable number of medical men are opposed to this idea and therefore it is not a good time to advocate a measure of this kind. I am ready to admit that medical men have done a great deal to cure and prevent disease, but I do not think we should take their judgment in such a matter as this as absolute. Like all of us, they have their own professional interests to consider. For example, it was found that in Great Britain medical men were not among those who were most keenly in favour of medical reform, nor were they among those most keenly in favour of the extension of social services by the state. The same thing has recently been found to be true in New Zealand, and I believe also in connection with health services in certain provinces of Canada. I do not think we should be asked to accept as decisive the opinion of a certain group of the medical men. I realize that there are many medical men who are in favour of state medicine, but we should not take the temporary decision of certain members of this profession as final.
Like everyone else, medical men are apt to think in terms of the days when they began to practise and when individualism was more or less the rule. Times have moved on. The leader of the opposition has said that years ago we saw the beginning of a new development when many large industrial companies

National Health-Mr. O'Neill
introduced collective medical services. That is all very well for those who are at work, but I would point out that there are large numbers of our people to-day out of work. There are also large numbers who are receiving such small wages that except in the most extreme emergencies they cannot call a doctor with any hope of paying for his services. Under these circumstances some form of health insurance or state medicine becomes very desirable. Some medical men from the narrower standpoint may be afraid of all that may be involved for themselves or for their profession in this idea, but as in many other instances I think it will be found that they will gradually fall in line with the new conceptions with regard to matters of social welfare.
Somebody has raised the question of where the money is to come from. May I suggest that unless we revert to barbarism, sooner or later the money in any case will come out of the community. It takes a lot of money to support our hospitals and health institutions of all kinds. Surely it would be more economical if we could prevent people from becoming ill. As I said the other evening with regard to crime, I think a greater proportion of the expenditures for penitentiaries and hospitals should be made to prevent crime and disease. Unfortunately we need these institutions at the moment, but we must not lose sight of the larger needs.
This brings me to the third consideration I had in mind. I have spoken about the desirability of periodical health examinations, and I have said that sooner or later we shall have to come to some form of state medicine, which would include medical health insurance. Perhaps more important than these is preventive medicine. We are gradually beginning to realize the desirability of preventing disease. It seems to me that there is absolutely nothing in the British North America Act to prevent the dominion government from going further along these lines than it has hitherto. In the old days we had to fight against smallpox, cholera and many of the great scourges of the middle ages, but even to-day there are other types of disease which take a heavy toll. I hope the government will give careful consideration to what may be done under modern conditions along more modern lines.
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops): Mr. Speaker, I think practically all hon. members will be found to be in sympathy with the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). We hear a great deal about dominion and provincial rights, about the British North America Act
and as to whether we have a right to bring into vogue a system of state health insurance, but I think in the last analysis public opinion will be found to be the force that will bring about state health insurance.
We have a hospital in Kamloops which was going behind all the time. At every annual meeting of the board of directors attempts were made to find some means to help the hospital. One of the lady members of the board happened to visit a small town in Saskatchewan where they had hospital insurance. She brought back the idea to Kamloops, where the idea was adopted and proved to be a great boon, not only to the people but to the hospital. The hospital is now for the first time in many years beginning to pay its own way, and the people are able to get hospital treatment at rates they are able to afford. They pay one dollar a month, which includes hospital care for the entire family.
In British Columbia also the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific have health insurance schemes of their own for their employees, who contribute $1.75 a month and receive free medical attention, free hospital treatment and free medicine. When these advantages can be secured by the employees of a railway I see no reason why they should not be provided in Ontario by the 'big manufacturing plants, where often you will find four or five hundred employees in one plant; or if you could not have such a plan in one plant, half a dozen plants could get together and make an arrangement with the doctors.
Further, in Ontario there is an organization formed by the doctors themselves, known as the Associated Medical Services Incorporated. In my opinion, a committee should be set up at this session to study this question in order to see if we cannot get the doctors to cooperate in formulating a plan for submission to parliament, which can then, if necessary, whip it into proper shape.
In British Columbia the provincial government made a conscientious effort to bring into force the state health insurance act which the legislature had passed, but it met with a great deal of opposition, and the opposition of doctors retarded the operation of the act. Therefore, I think it would be much better if we could get the doctors to formulate and submit to parliament a plan of their own, which parliament could use as a basis in enacting suitable legislation, than to have parliament initiate a plan the operation of which might later be blocked by the doctors. What I have said about the doctors in British Columbia I have said in no belittling sense. While they did not block the legislation, the
15S4

National Health-Mr. Needham
objections they raised were the greatest factor in retarding the operation of state health insurance in that province.
If nothing is done by parliament at this time to bring about state health insurance, at least every member, on his return to his section of the country, can try to get his constituents to adopt a scheme of health insurance and do the best he can to bring about state health insurance on a small scale in the local community, and then it will not be very long before public opinion will force this parliament, in spite of the British North America Act, if that should prove an obstacle, to enact legislation to bring into force state health insurance on a national scale.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
I shall say only a few words because I spoke to a similar resolution last year and I do not want to cover the same ground. I am speaking at the moment not as a medical man, but as one who has had a good deal of experience in the administration of a hospital, and I approach the question from the point of view of preventive medicine. In a hospital you come in contact with the individual who has been forced to undergo treatment in such an institution, and after he has left, you will perhaps hear one medical man saying to another: "If only that man had come to me five or six years ago I could have added ten or fifteen years to his life." But the reason why people do not go for an annual medical examination is largely a financial one; they are afraid of the cost. Some may be afraid that they will be told of some condition which they hope they do not have, and that deters people quite a bit from going to a doctor for medical examination.
I am in favour of this resolution, from the point of view of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), because I believe that more effective work can be done by cooperation between this government and the provinces. I am of the opinion that health is largely a provincial matter, and I believe that the provinces have gone and are going about as far as they possibly can in instituting state medicine. They would go even further if they had the necessary funds.
We have a minister of health in the dominion government, and in that way public health becomes a dominion issue. Reference has been made to what the municipalities are doing. Most of the provincial governments are placing responsibility on the municipality, leaving the municipality to look after the health of its citizens. They too are going just as far as they possibly can with the funds at their disposal.

There is one phase of the matter which I wish to emphasize from the dominion point of view. The dominion evidently has a responsibility to eveiy citizen of the state because it claims the life of every citizen if needed; in case of war, for example. We are expecting to have laid before us a large appropriation for defence purposes; I say that the surest and best defence that this Canada of ours can have is a strong healthy citizenship, and if we diverted some of the proposed defence appropriation to strengthening the health of our people I think we should have better results and there would be greater satisfaction throughout the dominion.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a few words to show that I am in sympathy with the spirit of the resolution. I think we have come now almost to the time when the people do not care whether health is a federal or a provincial matter. What they do care about is that it is a human matter. One hears people talking everywhere about the necessity for state medicine or health insurance or some way of taking care of the sick.
Everybody knows that one serious illness in a family, and not necessarily a poor family but a family that you might call between poor and well off, is enough to cripple that family for years. I know one instance in my own riding where a boy, one of two sons, contracted .a serious illness last July, and that one illness will actually cost those people all that they will make for years to come. We have heard a great deal about what, the doctors do to assist poor families. Nurses also help. I could not help thinking of the nurse who took care of this case of spinal meningitis and saved the boy's life and mind at a great risk to herself. If she is paid, it will be because the family will make a superhuman effort to pay her. It is a large family, some of the children being only five or six, and it will mean that they will have to do without necessities in order to pay the nurse. Nurses as well as doctors render great service to families who are unable to pay for the service.
I do feel that the federal and provincial governments should get together and decide who is responsible, and then move as rapidly as possible towards some sort of health insurance or state medicine-I do not think it matters what it is called. But I do think we have come to the time when we want to pay the doctors and nurses to keep us well. That would cost less and result in much greater happiness. There would also be an economic gain because there would not be

National Health-Miss Macphail
so much interruption of work. Certainly it is the human and civilized way of going about the matter and the sooner we do it the better. No matter how much preventive medicine or health insurance we may have, that alone, while helpful, will not eliminate all the causes of sickness, because in some areas, whether in the country or in the city, where the people have not the proper variety of food, where their food is monotonous and is not the sort that is needed for healthy bodybuilding, where they lack sunshine and air-flooded rooms, where there is no recreation or exercise of a kind to promote body-building, we are bound to have illness. So that much as I believe in doing something along the line of state medicine-and we shall not do it all at once-I suggest that there are other things that we shall have to do at the same time. We shall have to make changes in our whole economic and social set-up in order to do away with the great poverty from which so many Canadians suffer to-day.
When I was in Russia, I visited many of the free health centres, one type of which is called the mother-and-child clinic. In Canada we are accustomed to say a good deal against Russia, and I for one would not care to live there-I would rather live in Canada- but I was both delighted and surprised when I saw the care given to the health of the people. The whole of that vast country is covered by these clinics and various health centres. In one mother-and-child clinic I visited in Moscow I saw the children coming in. The mothers are taken care of through pregnancy and delivery; the child is brought to the clinic once a week until it reaches the age of four, and all this is done without cost to the individual or the family. The only cost involved is for some particular diet which the child may need, and if the parents are working and can afford it they are expected to provide it. If, however, parents cannot procure it, it is provided just the same. I went through the clinic, the house of a former prince, and at the back there was a receiving room. There were little individual compartments, something like telephone booths only larger, to which the children were taken. The doctor would look over the child to see whether it had any disease that could be communicated to children in the waiting rooms, and if it had the child was taken directly to its own home or to a hospital.
Another interesting thing I noted was that in the care of the child the same doctor followed its progress right through. In the mother-and-child clinic in which I spent a forenoon there were thirty-two doctors of
whom twenty-eight were women, and the same doctor would take care of a child from birth to the age of four. It was not any doctor who happened to come along; the child's progress was watched by the same doctor throughout that period. There are many such clinics all over that vast city and over the still vaster country.
With regard to the observations of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden),
I think many of these people who are ill should be getting some pay in the meantime if their minds are to be free enough to allow them to get well. In Russia when people are suffering from any illness, when workers, whether men or women, are sent to a sanatorium, they are paid the same wage as if they were at work so that they are not worried over their dependants during the illness of the bread-winner. That undoubtedly results in much more rapid cures than would result in Canada, where very often, when people are sent to a sanatorium, they do not know how in the world their families are going to get along, and they spend a good deal of time in worry which prevents them from getting well.
In connection with the great factories of Leningrad and Moscow, the majority of the doctors in the clinics attached to the factories are men, where the majority of the workers are men, and the majority of the doctors are women where the workers are women. We saw the creche where the mother leaves the child while she is at work. There the child is brought up scientifically with the greatest of care. Its food is carefully inspected, its sleep and even the toys with which it plays are supervised.
Coming out of Russia we passed through Denmark and Sweden, and I met the deputy minister of health of Denmark, and an official of the department of health of Sweden. I learned something of the benefits that accrue to the people of Denmark and Sweden from their nation-wide health insurance scheme. The people contribute a little bit all the time, and when they are ill they receive the very best care in the hospitals for two kronen and a half, which would not be more than sixty cents, a day. They get complete care in hospital, and that is not only nursing but medicine and surgical care as well. They would not think of reverting to a condition without health insurance. It has become a part of their lives and they would not dream of doing without it.
I believe that in Canada we are in many respects away behind other countries, not only in this particular matter but in many others as well. There does not seem to be
15S6
National Health-Mr. Kuhl

the same sort of public responsibility for the care of the sick and more particularly for the prevention of sickness, and it is time we moved. Surely we ought to be able to do something this session. If we had asked to have a committee set up to study the question it would have been better, but at any rate it is time the government moved. That is enough to give them a temperature, but still it is time that they themselves took responsibility and moved in the matter of health insurance or state medicine or some form of preventive medicine to help take care of people when they become ill.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
There is only one point on which I wish to place special emphasis. It is a foregone conclusion that we are all heartily in favour of providing more adequately for the health needs of the people of Canada, and it is also conceded by everyone that a nation can be strong only so long as its people are healthy and virile. These things should be and in fact they are taken for granted.
The point has been raised, and I think it is the only point in this whole discussion: How much will this health service cost, and how can we provide for it? There are two viewpoints from which we can look at the question. From the real cost point of view Canada can afford all the cost of providing the people of Canada with all health requirements; for, after all, what is the only real cost of providing or doing anything? It is human skill and energy, and physical material. In the final analysis that is the only real cost of doing anything anywhere. Surely it is obvious that Canada can provide all the things required to supply the people of Canada with all they need to raise their standard of health to the highest that is physically possible.
The financial side of the matter is merely bookkeeping. Surely if the people of Canada collectively can supply the real cost, it is the simplest common sense that we should set up a bookkeeping system, or so revise our bookkeeping system, that it will reflect what is physically possible for the people to do for themselves. What is the only real cost of building institutions? It is the building material-the brick, lumber, cement and whatever goes into the erection of the building-and the human labour to set it up. Certainly the people of Canada can provide all those things to erect institutions to care for the health of its people.
Furthermore, surely it is conceded that we have sufficient medical skill, sufficient doctors and nurses, or if not, they can be provided 
quickly. So from the real cost point of view the facilities necessary to provide for a high standard of health for the Canadian people can all be supplied. Then, why in the name of common sense should we not now arrange our bookkeeping system, our money system, to reflect these facts? That is the only real question in any problem that is raised in this parliament, or anywhere else. It would be conceded, I am sure, that physically we can solve almost any problem that faces this dominion. Every problem that is raised here eventually resolves itself into a question of finance, and until we set up an adequate financial or bookkeeping system it is in my opinion a waste of time to talk about these problems-

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
The resolution contains the clause "to provide periodical health examinations", which I think is extremely important. The public does not take advantage of its medical health officers. They are there to serve us. We have even had members of parliament drop dead who did not know they were sick. They should have known they had high blood pressure. Especially is periodical examination necessary for smaller children and for those over fifty years of age. The medical health officers should examine the public at a reduced rate as part of their jobs. Not only in cases of sickness do people need their advice, but you find sometimes big, fat fellows who perhaps do not know they are eating too much, and the health officer should tell such a man to diet, or tell his wife to stop feeding him. Or

National Health-Mr. Blair
a man might be found who shows every indication of having had, say too much beer. He should be told not to do so. Or if a man is working too hard he should be told, for the sake of his own life. This is no trivial situation, because people are dying on all sides who should not die, whose death might be prevented by a timely examination. It is generally believed that more people die from overeating than anything else, so it would be much cheaper to cut down on the diet.
I sometimes amuse myself watching the crowds go by and taking notes, and about every sixth or seventh person one sees is in obvious need of false teeth. Not having them means that these people will die that much sooner. In examining the mouths of the children in the public schools, which I have to do every year, one finds that their teeth are not attended to at all, they are growing in all shapes, the result being that their mouths are not in proper condition when the secondary teeth come in. We are not taking proper care of this generation. We do not think it is the duty of this house to take care of them.
We think there is unnecessary duplication of services. We have had travelling clinics sent out by this government going through the provinces, examining for tuberculosis, and other clinics are sent out by the provinces. That is folly. But we should have free travelling clinics for tuberculosis going through the country every year, under well organized provincial medical control and subsidized by the federal government. More attention should be paid to the services of the medical health officer, much more work should be required of him, and people should be compelled to go to the health officer so that he may guide them as best he can for their own benefit and for the purpose of prolonging their lives.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
resolution before the house reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government of Canada should try to secure amendments to the British North America Act, to provide periodical health examinations and provision for suitable treatment for all those suffering from disease.
This and similar resolutions that have been placed on the order paper during past years- I may say in increasing numbers in more recent years-indicate that the people of this country are more and more taking an interest in public health, and so far as I am concerned that is absolutely all to the good. In former days, as older members will recall, when a resolution of this kind came up there was usually a doctors' field day, and those of us who were lay members of the house rarely
ventured to discuss the question at issue. I am not sure whether our intervention would have been very welcome in any case. It is,
I think, an encouraging feature for those interested in public health that so many hon. members who are not by profession medical men should take part in these debates and endeavour to impress their views on their fellow members and on the Canadian people. In other words, the members of this house are becoming health conscious. Whether that is as a result of pressure from their constituents or whether for once we are taking the lead is not a matter of much importance; what I think is important to the people of Canada is that whatever methods or means we may adopt to achieve our object, we are coming to realize that those things'once considered purely idealistic, to which only visionaries subscribed a few short years ago, have now become almost matters of what I might call practical politics.
There has come to a very large number of people in this country the belief that every citizen is inherently entitled to as much right to protection from sickness and disease as to protection from the more violent if often less hazardous, attacks of those who wish to steal his property or injure his person. The great difficulty would not appear to be so much the acceptance of the principle. I believe we have placed behind us the view held in days gone by that sickness, disability and illness were each man's individual concern and that the calling of a doctor was something to be avoided except in the most extreme cases. In those days the doctor was one of the most unwelcome visitors to the home. Not only was he unwelcome when he came in the course of his professional duty; he was still more unwelcome later when he attempted to collect the fruits of his labour.
I think we have reached a stage where it is not difficult for anyone to obtain the undeniable sympathy of members of this house and of the country at large to almost any proposal for an increase in the amount of money to be spent on public health. The difficulty, I believe, lies first in regard to just what authority, municipal, provincial or federal, is to be charged with the responsibility of carrying out those proposals; and second, in spite of the advice we have received from some of my hon. friends in the far corner, just where we are to raise the large sums of money which inevitably will be involved in carrying out these highly sympathetic proposals.
I might digress here for a moment to deal with the suggestion of my good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with respect to that very point of the responsibility of the various auth-
National Health-Mr. Power

orities which deal with health in this country. On consulting part II of the act respecting the Department of Pensions and National Health, I find that the duties and powers of the minister are set out as follows:
The duties and powers of the minister under this part shall extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health of the people of Canada over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects:
(a)	Cooperation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities with a view to the coordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving and improving the public health, the conservation of child life and the promotion of child welfare

That was urged by my hpn. friend. Some of the other duties imposed upon the minister are these:
(b)	The establishment and maintenance of a national laboratory for public health and research work;
(e)	The inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen, and the administration of marine hospitals;
(d)	The supervision, as regards the public health, of railways, boats, ships and all other methods of transportation;
(e)	The supervision of federal public buildings and offices with a view to conserving and promoting the health of the civil servants and other government employees therein;
(f)	The enforcement of any rules or regulations made by the International Joint Commission. . . .
(g)	The administration of the acts mentioned in the schedule to this act-
That is to say, the Food and Drugs Act and others.
(h)	Subject to the provisions of the Statistics Act, the collection, publication and distribution of information relating to the public health, improved sanitation and the social and industrial conditions affecting the health and lives of the people;
(i)	Such other matters relating to health as may be referred to the department by the governor in council.
Section 12 of the act, however, considerably restricts the authority conferred upon the minister. It reads:
Nothing in this part or in any regulations made hereunder shall authorize the minister or any officer of the department to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial or municipal board of health or other health authority operating under the laws of any province.
So all we can do, so far as the provincial authorities are concerned, is cooperate. We have no power and no authority over them. Let us take for a moment the proposal with respect to periodical medical examinations, with which we are dealing at the present time. May I say at once, though perhaps this carries no authority, that from the informa-

tion I have been able to acquire in one way and another, officially and otherwise, I have been led to the conclusion that periodical medical examinations would be of great benefit to the community; first of all, by detecting and permitting the diagnosis in the earlier stages of diseases which might very well turn out to be fatal later on, such as cancer, heart disease and so on. It wrould be beneficial in observing the development of the individual and would permit us to detect the earliest signs of change from the normal and of impending disease. It would enable us to observe the effects of a hygienic daily regime; to note abnormal conditions arising from neglect of the laws of health; to recognize the benefit of following advice given to correct these abnormal conditions; to detect the early signs of focal infections and the results of their persistence; to accumulate facts regarding early symptoms of disease and treatment; to investigate the possibilities of cure in cancer, tuberculosis, venereal disease, et cetera, and to study the importance of hygienic and dietetic treatment in general. So that I do not think there is any difference of opinion [DOT] with respect to the value, not only to the individual and the community but to the dominion in general, of putting into effect something like periodical medical examination, in a general way.
If I may be permitted to digress again I would say that we have in this country to some extent periodical medical examination carried out gratuitously by the insurance companies. On January 1, 1930, a system of periodical health examination was adopted for the policy-holders of four insurance companies, namely the Sun Life, the Confederation Life, the London Life and the Canada Life. The scheme was inaugurated by the Canadian Medical Association. The companies agreed to pay $6 for each examination, $4 of which would be paid to the doctor and S2 to the Canadian Medical Association for administration and education. To further the scheme the Department of Pensions and National Health, in cooperation with the Canadian Medical Association, published a booklet for the guidance of physicians making examinations. In 1931 the number of policy-holders examined was 3,797. Having inaugurated the scheme the Canadian Medical Association dropped out, and its place was taken in 1931 by the Canadian Medical Institute of Toronto, which acted as administrative body.
The Canada Life Insurance Company has dropped out of the scheme, and at the present time there are three companies which have periodical examinations for policy-holders, namely the Sun Life, the London Life, and

National Health-Mr. Power
the Confederation Life. The examinations are confined to policy-holders thirty years of age and older, and for policies of $5,000 or more. In 1938 the total number of policy-holders examined was 6,000, and it is believed that in 1939 the number will be close to 7,000. Since 1931, 36,610 policy-holders have been examined. The fee paid at the present time to the examining doctor is $5, and the per capita cost of administration is $1.42, making a total of $6.42.
It is obvious that if periodical medical examinations were made available for all the people of Canada on the basis adopted by the insurance companies above-mentioned, the cost would be practically prohibitive. It might be possible to obtain a reduction in the medical fee if the numbers examined were sufficiently large, but no one could expect a doctor to make a thorough medical examination for less than $3. Even at this amount the cost would be still almost prohibitive. The only practical way, I am advised, to adopt a periodical medical examination would be by some system of health insurance.
But to return to the question of periodical medical examination, may I point out that in order to have the greatest value there would have to be some element of compulsion or coercion in it. Unless all, or almost all, or even a large majority, of the people of this country desired the examination, or were willing to give themselves the trouble or to suffer the inconvenience of calling on a selected medical man to be examined, some form of coercion would have to be employed. If we wanted to have a good cross-section indicating the health of the people of Canada in different localities, I am convinced this compulsion would have to be brought to bear.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would be the firdt to agree with me that he would not expect me, at any rate- and I do not think I would expect him, if he were in my place-to go to any province in Canada and say, "I ask you to permit me, or to permit the government of which I am a part, to amend the British North America Act, so that I may impose coercion on the citizens of your province and place upon them the obligation of coming before a doctor to be examined." I would thereby be violating the elementary principle of the British North America Act with respedt to civil rights. Then I would have to go one step farther. I would have to call on my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and ask him to lend me his mounted police, so that they could go forth into the country districts and round up or corral the recalcitrants who refused to have their teeth cleaned or their chests thumped.
I fear very much that my right hon. friend, with all the courage he has and all the desire he 'has to be of assistance to his fellow countrymen, would not undertake to enter into such a campaign as that-a campaign whereby we would have to apply some system of fine, coercion or force to bring the people before the doctors for examination.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is perhaps about to say that a large number of people would wish to be examined. The statistics we have from the insurance companies lead us to the conclusion that even in those companies, where this work can be done free of charge, where it is performed on those policyholders having policies of $5,000 or more, and where it can be performed without great inconvenience or loss, advantage has not been taken of the opportunity to anything like the extent to which it could have been taken.

I am not sure, but possibly we could set up centres in which all who wanted could have medical examinations. Admitting that is possible, I come to the next objection. After all, periodical medical examination would be only part of the great problem of looking after the health of the people. I will not say it is putting the cart before the horse or that it is an unimportant part of the problem, but I do contend it is not an absolutely first essential in the general health problem. It must be included in the general problem of health insurance, whether such a plan is contributed to by the municipality, by the province or by the federal government. Of itself I cannot see that it would be of much benefit unless there were other means of looking after those who, upon examination, were found to be ill. After all, w'e would not be getting very far if we simply set up examination centres where we could tell Bill Jones that he had a leaky heart, and advise him where to go for treatment. Necessarily we would be obliged to coordinate our efforts with those of the hospitals, with those

of the medical authorities generally in the provinces and with those of the provincial health authorities. All we could do would be to tell a man what his disability was and where he could obtain treatment.
I am speaking now to the resolution as it is drafted and am not discussing the general principle. I contend that if we adopted this resolution as it is drafted we would not get very far. If we are to undertake anything that would be of value to the people of Canada, we must coordinate our efforts with those of the provinces on a much wider scale. I would like nothing better than to be in a position to propose a bill similar to that introduced into the senate of the United States on February 28, 1939, by Senator Wagner of New York. subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just at six
o'clock the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) asked if it was possible to ascertain the proportion, of those who could if they wished obtain periodical medical examination from the insurance companies, who have actually taken advantage of this free benefit. I have not been able within the time at my disposal to ascertain the exact numbers, but I am reliably informed that only thirty per cent of the limited number, it is true, of those who hold policies of a value of over $5,000 have up to the present taken advantage of the offer made to them by the insurance companies.
In numbers it was something like 36,000 since the scheme was inaugurated in 1930, and this year it is expected that some 7,600 will take advantage of the offer.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that I have not very much more time at my disposal. I took up rather more time than I had intended in discussing some of the proposals which are now before the United States senate with respect to health generally and health insurance.
The house will remember that as far back as 1929 this house passed a resolution referring to the committee on industrial and international relations the question of sickness and invalidity insurance, and that committee reported to the house that the department of health should make some study of the question of health insurance in order to be prepared to give the information which would be necessary whenever the house or the country should desire that health insurance be put into effect. Time will not permit my placing on Hansard anything like the quantity of information which it has been possible to collect in the department, but if the house will bear with me for a moment or two I should like to sketch as briefly as possible some of the plans for health insurance or state medicine as they exist in different countries, and also to point out, with all due respect to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), who wished to abolish the department over which I now preside, that we have done something at least in gathering information to be available to members of the house and others who are interested in this matter, which information will guide them in their further researches in matters relating to state medicine and health insurance.
Last year, during the course of the debate on a similar subject, I dealt extensively with the situation as it exists in Russia, which is really the only country in the world that has state medicine in all its implications, and where, so far as we are aware, owing to their peculiar constitutional set-up, it has been found practicable so to regiment their medical men and their citizens that it is quite possible and even probable that state medicine has been successful.
In Germany they have a state insurance scheme, contributory and to some extent compulsory, and 19,000,000 citizens of that country come under its provisions.
In Norway the system of state health insurance is compulsory through insurance societies, which are confined one society to one district, and the division of contributions is made along these lines: The insured pays six-tenths; the employer, one-tenth; the commune, which I take to be the municipality, one-tenth, and the state, two-tenths.
National Health-Mr. Power

In Sweden, of which we hear a great deal these days, the system is voluntary, and here again it operates through societies with fixed societies in each region. The insured receives one quarter of the costs of medical care and drugs and has to pay for the rest of it himself. In Sweden one million persons out of a total population of 6,300,000 come under this scheme.
In Denmark the scheme is on a voluntary basis,. again through societies, but the state there pays fifty-four cents a year per head for persons whose income is less than a legally specified limit. So I take it that in Denmark what we might call the medically indigent are being looked after, and the state also gives cash for lay-off periods and provides for medical and maternal care. Out of a population of 3,700,000, there are 2,100,000 so insured.
In France they have a system all their own, whereby the sick pay out of their own pockets a percentage amounting to about twenty per cent of the doctor's medical costs, and the state provides a certain amount.
In Italy, while I have not been able to ascertain just how the proportion is made up, the fascist confederation of industry and the fascist confederation of industrial workers handle together the insurance of all the workers.
In Great Britain, as is well known, their health insurance scheme has been in effect for twenty-five years. Prior to 1936 there had been expended in insurance benefits $2,825,000,000, and there are in the reserve funds $618,270,000.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE HEALTH EXAMINATIONS AND TREATMENT FOR DISEASE
speechtext:
One of the more recent schemes has attracted a good deal of attention-the cooperative movement of the university of St. Francis Xavier at Antigonish. That went into operation on January 1, 1939, the unit being known as the mutual hospital group. There is a family rate of $2 a quarter. This will entitle members of the group to five weeks of ward treatment and a fifty per cent reduction in the rate for private and semiprivate rooms, together with laboratory services, ordinary medicine and a fifty per cent reduction on X-ray and operating fees.
In New Brunswick they have the Moncton group hospitalization service, in western Ontario, the Galt hospital service society, a nonprofit, cooperative hospitalization scheme, incorporated last year. A membership of 200 is the absolute minimum with which it would be safe to start. I have a note here that in no place in Canada or the United States where a hospitalization scheme of this kind has been properly thought out has it met with failure.
British Columbia has many such successful ventures. Directors of the King's Daughters hospital, Duncan, B.C., completed arrangements in December, 1938, for the inauguration of a hospital benefit scheme similar to those which are in successful operation in a number of districts in British Columbia. The scheme offers a contract whereby the contract holder and, if he is married, his wife and dependent children under twenty-one, may secure hospital accommodation and service, including stock drags, anaesthetics and the use of the operating room and X-ray equipment for a period of three months in any contract year. The annual payment has been set at $15, which may be paid in monthly instalments. To make the scheme successful and to get it under way it will be necessary for 1,000 contract holders to sign up. Kamloops has a successful scheme now operating. Kelowna also has a similar scheme.
We also have in Canada schemes of group medicine, to which reference was made this afternoon by a number of speakers. There is Associated Medical Services Incorporated, with headquarters in Toronto. In January, 1939, the chief medical officer of the corporation stated that subscribers in Ontario numbered over 4.300. Between June 1, 1937, when the association was formed, and September 1, 1938, approximately 1,400 accounts were paid, ranging from $1 to S150 on single items, to $400 in one case. The maximum allowed anyone in need of medical services is $800 in one. year. As each person is allowed to choose a doctor, the number of physicians who

work with the organization grows as the membership mounts. Membership costs $2 a month, plus $1.75 a month for the first dependant and $1.50 a month for each succeeding dependant. Most subscribers are in Toronto, but the plan is in operation also in Ottawa and in Norfolk and Oxford counties. The rate of growth has been continually increasing, having risen from a low of 193 in January, 1938, to a maximum of 525 in November, 1938. The annual subscription averages between $1.85 and $1.90 a month, depending on the average size of the family subscribing during the month. The average expenditure over the twelve months' period of 1938 for those entitled to service was $1.08 a subscriber per month. In Toronto there are approximately 820 participating doctors out of 950. In Ottawa there are 139 participating out of about 150.
These schemes are also in effect in some of the western provinces, in Saskatchewan and, I believe, in Manitoba. Also in western Canada there is a scheme known as the municipal doctor scheme. Perhaps some hon. members from Saskatchewan are far more familiar with the operation of this scheme than I can be, but in theory at least the plan is that a physician is engaged by the municipality on a salary basis to give the residents of the municipality medical care. In western Canada the municipality is the local unit of government, 200 to 300 square miles in area, with a population varying from 1,200 to 3,000. This type of service has extended until in 1938 over one-fifth of all the rural municipalities in Saskatchewan either have voted favourably on the scheme or were operating under a similar plan. In Manitoba there were in 1938 nine municipal corporations receiving medical care under the municipal doctor plan, with three or four more ready to initiate the scheme.
There are a number of other schemes for attaining the same object, persons in the community grouping themselves together in order to obtain greater benefits in the way of medical or hospital care.
There has been also an agitation throughout the country to press for what is known as state medicine, the definition of which I would take to be the furnishing by the state, free, of all medical, hospital, dental and other services. It has been stated pretty freely that a large number of the members of the medical profession would not care to join in such a scheme, partly, I assume, because some of the more prominent at least would not look with favour on the suggestion that they should all be state employees or servants of the state, and partly on account of the argument which has been

National Health-Mr. Power
set forth here on numerous occasions that there should be a particular and special relationship between patient and physician, which relationship is very difficult to achieve where the doctor is an employee of the state and liable at any time to be called upon to treat any patient. The cooperative schemes to a large extent overcome that difficulty, but in some countries it is overcome by giving the patient or the insured the right to choose his own doctor.
My view-and I express it here without endeavouring to hold the government in any way responsible for it-is that sooner or later all these schemes will have to be coordinated in some fashion under state supervision. I believe I should foe right constitutionally in saying that the supervising authority will not necessarily be the. federal authority, unless there is some change in our present constitutional arrangements. But the tendency is that sooner or later we must see to it that every citizen of the state obtains at least the minimum of medical care and attention.
The difficulty up to the present is that each province has looked at the problem from a different angle; what would be suitable in the way of health insurance for Quebec, for instance, would not apply equally well in British Columbia.. But once the provinces have themselves coordinated their efforts and come to the federal authority, I have no doubt that the pressure throughout the country will be such that the federal authority will be obliged to give leadership so that there will be put into effect a definite health program.
In passing, I may say that up to the present, although we have had our conferences with the provinces, it has been extremely difficult to bring all the provinces to see eye to eye as to what is the preferred procedure. Only recently I met the ministers of health of the various provinces. Some suggested that we should begin by attacking the problem of tuberculosis; others felt that the venereal disease problem was the one which should be handled at once; others thought that there should be full-time health units, and so on. It seems to me that the way to settle this matter definitely and to have a clear program which could be presented to the Canadian people would be by some kind of health conference at which there would be present representatives not only of the provinces as such but of social agencies interested in this kind of thing throughout the country, and medical associations, at which conference the particular interests of the provinces, of the dominion, of the medical associations and even of the welfare agencies, would be to some
extent set aside so that it would be possible without prejudice to determine what is needed as a beginning for the carrying out of our plan.
Of course I must not close without making some reference to the cost, because after all that will foe a factor in anything like a general scheme. It should be pointed out that just because a project is highly desirable does not necessarily mean that it is always economically feasible; and before such beneficial programs can be put into effect the cost must be counted so that there may be no subsequent regrets. I am not quite prepared to accept the suggestion, but it is often stated that just as soon as a form of state medicine is introduced the incidence of sickness will be doubled. If we introduce state medicine we will have to pay for it. Under state medicine the cost of medicine increases, and an instance is given here which I will mention, purely for the information of the house and not because I think it is what I would consider a conclusive argument. It states that, in the factory districts of England medicine costs are four times as large as in the district around Oxford university.
To return to the question of cost, as far as we are able to ascertain it in the 1931 census the cost of illness in Canada is $23 per capita. The cost of absolute state medicine would be at least $250,000,000 annually, with the suggestion that this cost would increase if all the services were free.

For some years, beginning in 1919, I believe, certain grants were made to the provinces in order to assist in combating venereal disease, on the condition that the provinces would set up clinics and contribute an equal amount. The grants continued-I am speaking subject to correction- for perhaps five years. Then they were decreased to $100,000 a year and finally, I think in 1931 or 1932, were cut out altogether. Last year they were revived in a different form when this house, as my hon. friend will perhaps remember, voted S50.000 in order to permit the federal government to supply arsenicals to the provinces to be used in combating venereal disease. So to all intents and purposes we have revived the contributions formerly made, perhaps on a smaller scale.
In conclusion I propose to repeat what I 3aid last year, that my personal view is that state medicine as such will not, for at least some little time, be generally accepted by She Canadian people. I feel that there is in it too much of regulation and regimentation to make it acceptable to the people of this country. But I also feel that some form of contributory health insurance will have to

be studied; and not only studied but put into operation in conjunction and cooperation with the provinces, before very long.
I want to thank the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) for having brought this matter to the attention of the house. We have had an interesting discussion; as I said at the outset of my remarks, we have heard the views of hon. members who are not directly connected with the medical profession but who feel that their constituents and the people of Canada generally want something to be done along these lines. Having obtained full approval of the principle of the proposal he wishes to lay before the people, perhaps my hon. friend will be satisfied to withdraw it, bearing in mind that perhaps in practice it would be extremely difficult to bring into effect exactly that which his motion, in its present phraseology, calls for.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker,' there are perhaps one or two misunderstandings that should be cleared up. Those who have need of these health examinations are neither the very poor nor the very rich, but rather the small wage-earners. I appreciate the discussion we have had to-day; I think it will indicate to the minister that this is a live question. For myself, whether within or without this house, while I am spared I am not going to let up in my efforts, because I see the need. When it is suggested that people will not attend for these examinations, might I say that anyone who attended the meetings of the municipal league of Thunder Bay district could not be there very long when this question was under discussion without finding out how they feel about it. There is no sham; it is a real issue. The low wage-earners and farmers are those who are in great need. I appreciated the frank statement of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), but I do not think he is altogether correct when he says the doctors do not want this. Thank you, doctor; or I mean I thank my hon. friend. I am not discussing state medicine. The resolution is very simple. I took heart as I listened to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), and I was also encouraged when I saw a photograph of the various

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Heaps
provincial ministers of health. I thought they were human, intelligent beings, and that when they would realize the need for what I have suggested they would have brains enough to put it into practice. We have provincial police protection and we have education which is paid for by the province. I think health insurance, or something of that kind-it may be called state medicine, or whatever you like -is most important.
When I go to the experimental farm I see our specialists experimenting to develop plant and vegetable life, and they are attempting to develop horses and cattle to the highest point of efficiency. What is our greatest asset in Canada? Is it not our men, women and children? I am sure the Minister of Pensions and National Health will understand me when I say it is more important to raise healthy men, women and children than it is to have thoroughbred horses.
I appreciate very much the time the minister has devoted to the subject. He has shown that he is capable of filling in the best possible way the position he holds. We wish him the greatest success in his endeavours. I am sure that if, when he is discussing this question in conference with representatives from the provinces, or when an effort is made to revise the British North America Act-and when we went to the country we promised it would be revised-he needs any help from the humble representative of the constituency of Fort William, I shall be there to work to the best of my ability.
As the minister has indicated, I do not think any useful purpose would be served by putting the resolution to a vote. In our own consciences we know where we stand, and so does the minister. For these reasons I beg to withdraw the motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. HEAPS (Winnipeg North) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Whereas it is becoming more and more difficult for older persons to be absorbed into the useful productive life of the dominion, thereby being unable to maintain themselves in decency and comfort;
And whereas Canada is a country richly endowed with natural resources capable of maintaining our whole population in a reasonably high standard of living;
Therefore be it resolved, that this house would welcome a government declaration of policy that would bring about an immediate lowering of the present pensionable age limit of seventy years, the effect of such being that
the older generation would retire from industrial activity, thereby creating opportunities for the younger generation to be usefully and gainfully employed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the third motion along these lines I have introduced in the last four sessions of parliament requesting that the pensionable age, now placed at seventy years, be reduced from that figure. Probably, on my third effort, my insistence or persistence in the matter may be a little more successful than it has been on the two previous occasions.
Before dealing directly with the motion, however, there are one or two observations I should like to make in regard to the present administration of the Old Age Pensions Act.
I am receiving complaints from many parts of Canada in regard to the stringent methods being applied in some of the provinces in respect of those who believe they ought to come under the provisions of the act. I have no intention this evening of dealing with certain of those complaints, further than to say that when the estimates are before the committee, I shall place those complaints before hon. members.
There is one complaint, however, I do wish to bring to the attention of the house, and particularly to the attention of the responsible minister, and it is that in some of the provinces the pensioners entitled to the full pension of S20 a month are not receiving the full amount. That is a serious complaint to make, and represents a serious hardship that is being visited upon pensioners in certain parts of the dominion. I believe this is particularly so in Saskatchewan. I say that when the House of Commons determined a pensioner should be entitled to a pension of $20 a month, it meant $20 a month. When in the administration of the act provinces allow a maximum pension of only $15 a month, I claim that the old age pensioners in those provinces are being deprived of S5 a month. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) disagrees with what I am saying. I am not accusing the federal government of responsibility for the reduction in the amount of the pension. On the other hand I say, clearly, that it is being done by those who are responsible for administration in some of the provinces. In view of the fact, however, that the Minister of Finance seems to dissent from the statements I make, perhaps I should read a letter which otherwise I had not intended to read at this juncture.
The letter I have in my hand is from the commissioner of old age pensions in Saskatchewan, and is dated December, 1938. I do not
