Then, if it is being done in other provinces I am glad I have drawn the attention of the minister and the house to it. It is a practice which ought to be stopped, and old age pensioners, whether they are single or married, ought to be entitled to the full amount of their pensions.
[Mr. Heapi.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Quite a number of provinces do not think so, and I find it rather difficult to make them.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I do not wish to enter into any extended argument on the point. The act specifies that a person who is in receipt of an income of not more than $125 a year, is entitled to a maximum pension of $20 a month. If those persons have qualified they are entitled to the full $20, and not to only $15. Again I claim that in Saskatchewan, or in any province carrying out this procedure, there is an evasion of the act, and I hope that in due course, with the assistance of the Minister of Finance, those old people who are entitled to $20 a month may receive the full amount of their pensions. However, when the estimates are before us, perhaps we may be able to go into that aspect of the question a little more fully than I intend to go into it to-night. I am just drawing this matter to the attention of the minister, and perhaps some good will accrue as a result of the remarks I have made on this question.
I stated a moment ago that this is the third occasion in four years that I have introduced a motion asking for a reduction in the pensionable age. I find no greater justification for my motion than the remarks made a few moments ago by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power). He gave particulars of what was being done in other countries in connection with old age pensions and referred to New Zealand, Australia, Great Britain, the United States and one or two other countries. We find that all of these countries are far in advance of Canada with regard to social legislation. I would go so far as to say that Canada is in this respect practically the most backward of the English speaking nations of the world. I do not say that with any degree of satisfaction, far from it. I would much prefer to be able to rise in my place in this house and say that Canada was the most advanced country in the world in regard to its social legislation.
I am pleased to note that to-day old age pensions are a part of the social structure in every one of our provinces. They have been accepted as a part of the economic life of the whole dominion. I do not think there is a province which would think for one moment of going back on its old age pension legislation. There . might be the odd person here or there with antiquated ideas, whose mind belongs to the bygone ages, who would want to see our old age pension legislation discontinued or its advance stayed, but they are few and far between. I believe the overwhelming majority of the people of Canada

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Heaps
are not only satisfied with the pensions we have at the present time, but extremely anxious to have the benefits of old age pensions extended to people below the age of seventy.
When this question was raised in the past two or three years, the minister expressed in a general way his sympathy with the proposal. I believe that in a sense every hon. member sympathizes with the idea of reducing the pensionable age from seventy to either sixty or sixty-five years. At first I asked that it be reduced to sixty years, but I am quite prepared to compromise with the government and accept, on the present occasion, a reduction to sixty-five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: That is typical of my hon. friend's Scotch extraction.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I hope the Minister of Finance will not be so Scotch as to refuse my modest request. On a previous occasion the minister told us that persons over the age of sixty years were fairly well off. He stated they were receiving on an average of about $1,076 a year by way of salary or wages. If that were the case there would be very few people of the age of sixty years or over who would require pensions. But the fact is that the overwhelming majority of those of the age of sixty years or over are finding it extremely difficult to get along and perhaps do not know where the necessities of life are to come from. Despite the fact that the minister is extremely sympathetic to the proposal, I feel sure he will tell us to-night what he has told us on other occasions. He will tell us about the cost and of the necessity for taking from those who have to give to those who have not. Then he may again ask the question: Where is the money to come from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree that it has to come from the people.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Now that the minister has
raised that question, I shall deal with it. When the minister raised this point a couple of years ago I stated that if money were required for the purpose of war, there would be no difficulty in finding funds. In 1936 the minister stated he could not find sufficient money to finance the payment of pensions at an age lower than seventy years. I would point out to him that to-day there has been an increase in the cost of our armaments to an extent greater than would have been required to pay pensions at sixty-five years. If we can find money for the purpose of armaments which will be utilized sooner or later to destroy life, I feel we ought to be able to find money for the purpose of conserving life.
It is said that this is taking money out of the pockets of the taxpayers; but where do 71492-101
the taxpayers get their money? Do they not get it from the goods or the wealth produced each year in Canada? I remember in 1930 when the house was called to a special session to vote $100,000,000, mostly for the purpose of dealing with the unemployment problem which was becoming worse and worse as the months went by in that year. Of that $100,000,000, a total of $20,000,000 was to be expended for purposes of direct relief. At that time we had more wheat in our granaries in western Canada than we knew what to do with. Our farmers were burning grain because they could not afford to buy coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: That was only an isolated case.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: But it happened. They were burning grain for fuel, while the miners in Alberta were wondering where their next meal was going to come from.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
How much wheat
was burned?

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I am making my argument
and my hon. friend can make his later on. The government of that day wanted $20,000,000 for direct relief when we had more foodstuffs and more food and shelter than we knew what to do with. The government went to New York and borrowed the $20,000,000, I believe from the house of Morgan, although it makes no difference. When they had borrowed that $20,000,000, our miners and our farmers could eat and obtain fuel. Could there be anything more ridiculous than an economic set-up which demands that we get permission from the bankers of Wall street before our farmers and miners of western Canada-the same thing applies all over Canada-can consume commodities produced in this country? When the minister asks: Where does the money come from-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I did not ask it.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
The minister asked it two
years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I said I thought we would all agree that it had to come from the people. I was not going any further than that by way of a discussion of where the money was to come from.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
It has to come from the people of the Dominion of Canada; but the people do not care whether they get a slip of paper or something else, what they want is food, clothing and shelter. I claim that at the present time we have in this country sufficient food, clothing and shelter to provide a reasonable state of existence to all our people of

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Heaps

the age of sixty-five years and over. If we did not have that abundance in our midst I would state immediately that I would not feel justified in asking this house to pass a resolution calling upon the government to give to our older people the right to sweet content, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would say, when they reach the age of sixty or sixty-five and over. After all, when a person reaches that age, the chances of being aibsorbed into industry are exceedingly slim. Where can a man of sixty-five or over find employment to-day? We have at the present time tens upon tens of thousands of our younger people who have not as yet been absorbed into useful productivity in the dominion. So what opportunity is there for a man of sixty-five or over to be able to find useful employment in Canada? Does it not seem absurd that our older population should be working when young men and young women in their teens and early twenties are walking about idle?
I have said that on two previous occasions I had a similar resolution on the order paper, but on both occasions it was talked out. The minister claimed that it was not possible for the government at that particular time to give to our older people a pension at a lower age than is now provided. I feel sorry for the government for the stand which it took, because the Minister of Pensions and National Health pointed out a few minutes ago that it is only a question of time before other social legislation of a similar nature will be enacted and put upon the statute 'books, and I think it would be a good thing from the point of view of the government for them to come forward with a definite statement that they will, if not at this session, at another session, grant the request I am now making and give to our older people some real hope that pensions will be granted in the near future at a lower age than is the case at present.
When I put that request in the form of a motion, all I am asking is that there be a fair distribution of our wealth production in this dominion. I do not want to take anything away from anybody. I do not even covet the wealth of those who have riches at the present time, because I believe that we can produce to-day in such abundance that we can give a fairly high standard of living to every Canadian within the confines of this dominion.
I shall read just a few lines from a pamphlet which may be recognized by some hon. gentlemen in this chamber. I shall not read it word for word, but will change a word here and there:
Our party recognizes that the problem of ilistribution has become more important than -hat of production, and believes that personality 
is more sacred than property. Our party will devote itself to finding ways and means of effecting a fair and just distribution of wealth with increasing regard to human need, to the furtherance of social justice, and to the promotion of the common good.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that every member of our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, and I have no doubt my friends to my left, will subscribe to the few words I have just quoted.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: My hon. friends of the Social Credit party say '"hear, hear." I wonder if hon. gentlemen of the Liberal party would bn just as willing to subscribe to these views as members of the Social Credit group or of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I have not yet heard any loud shouts from the Liberal party opposite. May I say that I have just quoted from a speech which the Prime Minister uttered in this House of Commons on February 27, 1933.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
He was in opposition
then.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Old age is becoming a more serious problem in some ways than unemployment. After all, when a young person in his twenties or thirties is out of work he has seme hope of some day being a little more fortunate and finding employment. But when a person advances along in years and old age begins to creep upon him, we find that he is not wanted in the labour market and his opportunities for a livelihood become more and more restricted as time goes on. When we see the figures of the numbers who are in receipt of old age pensions to-day, and the vast number of people in this dominion now over the age of sixty, we realize what a complicated and difficult problem old age is really becoming.
There is another problem in connection with old age that arises out of the advancement of medical science. The expectancy of life to-day is becoming greater and greater, and as it increases and people live longer they find it more difficult to earn a livelihood. Consequently the question of old age is one that I think ought to be dealt with in such a definite way as to give some hope to the older people of the dominion.
It may be said that if we give pensions to those of sixty or sixty-five years of age we do away with the incentive of what the Minister of Finance might call that good old Scotch habit of thrift.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
It is not only a Scotch habit.

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Heaps

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
No, but I thought the minister might have called it that. I mention that fact because to-day the average worker is not in a position to save very much out of the wage he receives. The average wage to-day is so low that very few people, comparatively speaking, receive what might be termed a saving wage. May I interject here that a good many of the figures we quote as to wages in Canada are not altogether as accurate as we would like them to be, for the simple reason that when our bureau of statistics gives us the annual wage, it shows what w'ould be earned if the worker were engaged for a full year, but the great majority of our working people do not work the full year but have periods when they are on shorttime.
I believe that our aged people to-day are entitled to their pensions not as a matter of charity, as some peoiple look upon old age pensions now, but as a matter of right in just exactly the same way as a pension is granted to a judge or a general. I believe that those workers who have given of the best years of their lives to build up our social structure in this dominion are entitled to the old age pension in the same way as our soldiers and judges, many of whom to-day are in receipt of exceedingly large pensions.
My plea this evening is for economic security for our older population. When men and women have given of the best years of their lives in building up the state and providing for others in the community,, I believe they are entitled, when they reach old age, to a measure of economic security which they do not have to-day until they reach the age of seventy. We have to-day at the present time, as has been pointed out time and time again in this house, an abundance of everything in this dominion. It is not a question of production; this has been solved; it is now a question of distribution. I do not think it is beyond the ingenuity of members of this house or of the government to devise ways and means whereby there can be a fairer distribution of our wealth production so as to provide adequately for people in their old age. It is often said that there is a great deal of discontent in this country, but the surest way of removing social discontent, as has so often been pointed out, is to give to our people that economic security which to-day is denied them to a large extent.
I am sorry to think that whereas in practically every part of the British empire old people are to-day receiving pensions at a much lower age than seventy-at the age of sixty-five, and in some parts at sixty-we in Canada can give pensions only at the age of seventy.

But in New Zealand and Australia pension schemes have been in operation for approximately thirty years. I do not believe they have been entirely on a contributory basis. However, if the minister has the facts I hope he will give them to the house when he speaks. In New Zealand the act has been widened to an enormous extent under the new legislation which has not yet become operative. There the minister will find that provision is made for pensions at the age of sixty. However, I say this to the Minister of Finance. If he finds fault with the act either in New Zealand or in Australia-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I am not finding fault.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Oh, I thought the minister
was finding fault. At any rate I am prepared to accept, so far as Canada is concerned, exactly the provision that Australia and New Zealand have made with regard to pensions. If they can give these benefits to the older people in Australia, New Zealand, the United States, Great Britain and many other countries which I could enumerate, why can we not do the same in Canada? Why should we lag behind other nations in our social legislation? There is no reason in the world, because we are in no way poorer than they. In fact, Australia carries a tax burden somewhat greater than we do, and they are prepared to shoulder their full responsibility when it comes to social legislation. If those countries are prepared to shoulder the
Old Age Pensions-Mr. Leader

responsibility of advanced social legislation there is no reason why we should not do the same.
There is no use in saying that this is a matter for the provinces or that the cost will be so great. I do not think that is a valid excuse. The people of Canada are prepared to-day to take a long step forward in the matter of social legislation, and I trust that when the minister speaks he will give us a more definite assurance than we have so far had, that in the immediate future the old people of Canada may look forward to having pensions at a much lower age than seventy as at present.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
In the first place I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) upon his persistence in bringing this motion before the house session after session. At one time I took exception and was not willing to lend my support to his resolution for the reason that he had scaled the age limit down from seventy to sixty, and I did not believe that Canada could afford to pension off old people at the age of sixty. However, I have almost come to the conclusion that we could do that. Perhaps I should put it in this way, that we should do that, for the reason that I am getting older myself and am looking forward to the day when I might be eligible for an old age pension.
To-night I want to say that I will support the hon. gentleman's resolution. It begins:
Whereas it is becoming more and more difficult for older persons to be absorbed into the useful, productive life of the dominion-
I agree with that. We who knock around among our people know that is absolutely true. We find so many people out of employment. Many sturdy young men are looking for jobs which they cannot find and we sympathize with them, but we sympathize far more with the older men who are unable to secure positions. We could quite well grant them a pension of $20 a month to help them in their old age. The second part of the resolution reads:
And whereas Canada is a country richly endowed with natural resources capable of maintaining our whole population in a reasonably high standard of living-
I agree with that also. We like to say that this is the grandest country in the world and that we have the greatest natural resources of any country. Then why not use them for the uplift of the people who live in Canada? The resolution goes on to say:
-that this house would welcome a government declaration of policy that would bring about an immediate lowering of the present pensionable age limit of seventy years.

My opinion is that the government should lower the age limit to sixty-five. The hon. member mentioned that old age pensioners were not receiving the full $20 a month allowance. I can vouch for the truth of that statement from my own experience. I know of one pensioner who was granted only $15. On making inquiries I found that this particular pensioner, a woman, was keeping house for a relative; it was thought that her services in that capacity were worth something and so the administration at Winnipeg decided to limit her pension to $15. I am glad to say that when I took the matter up with the commissioner in Winnipeg, it was rectified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think it just that some person should get the services of that old lady, make her work, and not pay her? That is one of the major abuses.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I take this stand most definitely, that if she was entitled to $20 a month it does not matter where she was living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: That is not what the resolution advocates.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: I am glad to say that the matter was rectified and she is now getting her pension of $20 a month. I know her personally and I can say that no one in this dominion is more entitled to that pension than she is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: My hon. friend is taking me up wrong. I am not saying the old lady was not entitled to it. But I say that those who were getting the benefit of her services as housekeeper should be made to pay for them. And I stick to that.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I disagree with the minister in that regard. I claim that if she is entitled to that $20 a month she should get it whether she works or not.
I want to deal to-night with two or three questions that have been asked me by my constituents. Some point out the inequality of our pensions and say that judges, if they retire after fifteen years' service, are granted pensions at two-thirds of their salaries, which may amount to $10,000 a year. They point out that these judges may live in any country in the world and still retain their right to the pension. I know as a fact that it is being paid under such circumstances, while if old age pensioners leave Canada for thirty days their pension is immediately cut off

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Leader
until they return. I have no fault to find with the law that compels a Canadian to live in Canada if he is drawing a Canadian pension; but that is where the inequality comes in, it should apply to every Canadian pensioner, to the judges of our higher courts as well as those receiving old age pensions. It is inequalities like that which cause so much unrest; that is why people are say-in, "What is the matter with democracy?" I could tell about a certain judge who was getting a pension of $6,000 a year; his last year's salary at the expense of the taxpayers of this country was $30,000, and he refused to pay income tax on it. He was assessed $9,000 on that $30,000 gratuity as he called it, but it was remuneration; he refused to pay, and the courts of this country upheld his contention. Is that justice?

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: It is democracy as it is operated to-day.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I brought up in this house the question of the returned men, who went to France and offered their all, were wounded, buried in shell holes, and after three years' service were so anxious to get out of the army and get home that although they had a disability the dead-line was reached before they put in their application. I know one man who has not reached the age at which he is entitled to the veteran's allowance. He is able to drive a school van that takes the children to school and thus make a few dollars a month, and he is denied a pension. I am not suggesting that our pension law in regard to our returned men has not been very liberal, but that is one case and perhaps there are thousands throughout this dominion in the same position. It is so hard for those returned men, who offered their all, to get a pension, yet a judge who does not need to worry is relieved by the courts of even having to pay income tax, and he does not have to live in Canada, whose people pay the pension.
Let me come back to those old age pensioners who are perhaps destitute, yet, who, because they have some relatives who are able to assist them to a limited extent, have the amount of that assistance deducted from their pension. I say again it is not right. Those people are entitled to that $20 a month, and it is not right to oblige them to look to their families to support them. If the family have enough pride-and many of them have-to keep their father or mother from getting the old age pension, that is all right, but if they have not enough pride, or perhaps enough money, that is no reason why these
people should not have every dollar of that pension which has been granted them by the laws of this country.
Another question that has been asked me is why the pension is cut off when the recipient leaves Canada. I knew an instance where a certain pensioner left Canada to visit some relatives in California, and when the authorities found out he was away, his pension was promptly cut off and he had to do without it for the time he was away. I do not find any fault with that, but I am coming to another illustration. We had a judge in my own city of Portage la Prairie who for twenty years lived in California but drew his pension of $3,000 a year. I believe he has died recently, but for nearly twenty years he was being paid $3,000 a year by the taxpayers of Canada while living in a foreign country.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):

While it seems that progress along this line is disappointingly slow, I do believe we are making some progress, at least as far as the general public is concerned, and possibly even in this house. I think back some years to the time when the old age pension legislation was put on the statute books. It was done with the greatest difficulty against the strongest possible opposition. We were told of the constitutional difficulty. Sticklers for the constitution said it was simply impossible to carry out any such scheme under the British North America Act. There was much the same kind of argument as the one we had to-day with regard to state medicine. As a matter of fact, although several of the provinces stayed out at first, one by one they came in until today they are all in. This notwithstanding what was said a few years ago about the constitutional difficulty, and their determination to boycott the whole scheme. Quebec, from which we have the most strenuous objections, has finally joined the other provinces.
So we were told it was absolutely impossible to finance this scheme. Well, it has been in operation for some years now. All the provinces are in; there has been a very large increase in the number of persons coming under the scheme, but this country is not quite bankrupt. Even if it is nearing bankruptcy that is not because of the claims of the old age pensioners.
Then we were told that we should not introduce this scheme for high moral reasons. I recall very well hearing it said in this house that by paying old age pensions to people of seventy we would be encouraging shiftlessness, that if they were sure of getting an old age pension at seventy no one would save. Further we were told that it would practically break up the family, because it was the duty of the children to care for their aged parents, and if those parents were looked after by the state the consequence would be that the children would not love their parents any more.

Apparently they were afraid they

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Woodsworth
would not go to heaven 1 We were warned of all these dire consequences, but such objections have all been swept away. Some of the people who made those objections have gone to their own reward, but still the scheme goes on.
We must remember that conditions have changed from the old days. I can remember when I was a child frequently seeing an old man sitting by the fire, or an old lady sitting in her cap and gown; my own grandmother, if you will. Many of us can recall such scenes. Who would begrudge the old gentleman or the old lady the little bit of food required or the clothes they wore? And they wore their clothes for a very long time in those days. To-day conditions are quite different, even on the farms, particularly those of the west which I know best. There are very few of these family farms where the old people can sit in comfort by the fireside. On the majority of the farms of the west that condition does not exist. Certainly when you come to the cities you find people who, in seeking work, have shifted from place to place. Most of the western people came either from eastern Canada or from overseas. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) knows as well as I do that they have moved from place to place, so that in many instances they have no long established residence. That, of course, is particularly true in the industrial centres. Under these changed circumstances we must adopt new methods. We must care for these people who did the pioneering in this country and who surely are just as worthy of being looked after as any other class in the community.
My hon. friend the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) spoke very strongly with regard to judges. One might refer also to civil servants, some of whom get quite tidy pensions. One might refer to the senate, where many former members of this house are now enjoying a comfortable salary in their declining years. The distinction between civil servants or judges or members of the senate on the one hand and farmers and industrial workers on the other is rather arbitrary. I assume they have all contributed to the upbuilding of this country, but why is it that simply because a man belonged to one particular class or was fortunate enough to be placed in a certain recognized position he is well looked after in his old age, while other people who in their own sphere have worked just as faithfully and done just as much for the upbuilding of this country have to pass a miserable old age?
Now I should like to say a few words with regard to the present administration of old age
pensions. In this instance I am glad not to have to criticize the dominion but must criticize rather the provincial governments. As my colleague said, I do not think the provincial governments are living up to the terms of the act, which laid down that under certain conditions the pension should be $20 a month. I do not 'believe any provincial government has the right to reduce that amount to $15. The act provided that people might have an income of $125 from other sources and still receive that $20 a month. That provision has not been lived up to in a great many instances, and it seems to me the dominion government should bring pressure to bear upon the provinces. After all, the provinces did not enact the Old Age Pensions Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Oh, yes, they did, in each province.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Yes, they passed supplementary legislation, but it was an act o: this parliament that laid down the conditions. We passed the primary legislation and the provinces, if they came in as " partners," to use the phrase of the Minister of Finance, came in on the terms of the dominion act. It seems to me if they are not willing to come in under those terms they should stay out. Then each province could settle the matter as to whether or not that particular government should remain in office. I want to protest against the badgering of old people and against the cheese-paring policy that is so often followed in connection with old age pensions. I should like to read a letter from my own constituency, dated March 3, which has just come into my office and which is typical of scores I have received. I had not time to have this letter copied, but will try to make out the writing:
In reference to old age pensions no doubt you are aware that a great majority are not receiving the full amount, namely twenty dollars. For instance in my case I receive fifteen and a quarter monthly. I was seventy on the first of May, 1938, but I did not receive my first cheque until the first of October, so you realize they have not given me the months intervening, a matter of five months. I have learned the fault lies with the Manitoba government. I have lived permanently in Manitoba for the last thirty-two years, had a lot of sickness and unemployment. I never had a banking account. I borrowed money on my home when my sons came home from the last terrible war. They were gassed and they were unemployed for a long time. They do not receive any pension. I really do consider this should have been the government's responsibility. I have never been able to get relief and have not been able to pay off the mortgage. . . . To further complicate matters we are obliged to give names of sons and sons-in-law for further particulars with a view to get them

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Woodsworth
to support us. Possibly I see in this a move to lessen our pension. Why should these young people be further penalized? The social welfare do all the investigating, nothing but highly organized spies. I think it cruel for poor old people to be subjected to so much obnoxious embarrassment.
The letter continues, but that is the gist of it. I heartily agree with the writer of that letter. It seems to me provision could be made to eliminate this constant interference with the privacy of the lives of people who have to accept old age pensions. I do not 'believe the investigators should have any right whatever to attempt to force the sons and other relatives to take over the responsibility for the care of these old people.
As my colleague has said, with the productivity of this country we ought to be able to lower the age and also raise the amount that is to be paid. I believe that to-day almost all people are living under higher tension than that under which people used to live. They are not able normally to carry on as long as many of those who lived in the quieter days of long ago. They may indeed live, but they are not fit for active hard work. We all know that there are many people in business and professional life who are turned off at sixty. What is there for such to-day?
Some of us who are rapidly approaching the age of sixty-five may be still able to do intellectual work. But I think of a good many of the men and women whom I knew as children. Many of them have dropped out. Those who were engaged in physical work are not able to carry on. Those who went farming are not as active as they used to be years ago. If they are on their own or their children's farms they putter around doing chores. In industry very few are actively engaged in jobs after they have reached the age of sixty. According to the old scriptural phrase a man's allotted years are three score and ten or, by reason of strength, four score years, then he passed on. Only at three score and ten years do we give him a pension, though he is probably played out at three score!
There is a big gap between sixty years, beyond which very few are able to secure work-especially manual work-and the age of seventy years at which they become eligible for old age pension. In these years, what are they to do? I can speak with the greatest assurance about the west. There are thousands in my own city who cannot get work at the age of sixty. What are they to do during the next ten long years? A great many of them are now on relief. Why should they not [Mr. Woodsworth.)
have some little security for their old age. I have read already a letter which came to-day. Within the last week I received another letter from a lady of sixty-six years of age who recalled that we had gone to school together in Brandon when we were children. This lady taught school in the rural sections of Manitoba during most of her life. To-day she is on relief. At her age she cannot get a school. For one or two years recently she did go out in an extremely backward district, at which time, owing to the extreme cold and the poor accommodation she was able to obtain, she contracted physical troubles. To-day she finds it next to impossible to get a school. What is she to do? I can remember the time in the old days when she lived with her mother. Many women helped to support their old mothers, and helped to send their brothers and sisters to school.
Sometimes in the comfort of this chamber we forget the conditions under which many people must live. Here is a lady who has carried on a useful life. She is not eligible for pension. At the age of sixty-six she finds herself compelled to wait for several long years, probably on public relief. Then she will be eligible for $20 a month-another kind of charity. She will have to swear up and down that she has nothing coming in. She will be investigated and badgered by officials. This, instead of receiving an old age pension as her right, because she has helped to build up the country.
As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has said, I think we ought not to have such great inequalities in the manner in which we deal with people. Older people ought to be dealt with as I am sure all hon. members would feel like dealing with them, if they were dealing with them personally. We would treat them with a certain dignity and recognize the work they have done in the past. We would give them a pension, not as a matter of charity, not as a bit of wretched relief, but give generously-something more than $20, something more than a miserable $15 for the one who is unfortunate enough to have a husband or a wife surviving! What after all, is $25 a month to an old man who has done his bit in the building up of Canada? How would we treat our own fathers and mothers if we had the chance? Why not act thus toward others? Why not do as much for other people, many of whom are equally worthy, but have not had as good an opportunity in life?

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Mutch

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I rise to support the motion as it appears on the order paper I hope it will not be interpreted as an endorsation of all that has been said by others who are supporting the motion. It is perhaps a little peculiar that we have wandered away from the actual subject of discussion to a consideration of real or imaginary grievances in connection with the administration of the act. Since that administration lies in the provinces I do not propose to spend any time in discussing it to-night.
This is the third time I have risen in the house to support a resolution lowering the age at which old age pensions may be given. The government have accepted the age of sixty-five as that at which we might reasonably be expected to retire from labour. Although they have accepted that in practice, they continue to deny it in principle. Consequently we have this situation of once more postponing that which is inevitable. I wish it were possible, particularly in connection with social legislation which is recognized as inevitable, that we might meet the inevitable now. I do not see why it should not be possible at this session not only to consider the advisability of immediately lowering the age for old age pensions from seventy to sixty-five years, but to give something more than cursory consideration to the possibilities of old age pension which under a contributory scheme might provide optional ages of retirement.
I am not one who thinks that by cutting a man off at the top, putting him on a form of government subsistence, and bringing in a younger man at the bottom we are creating another job. I hope I have sense enough to know we do not do that. But what is much more important is that at least we give a measure of security to a man who during his lifetime has made a contribution. We take him at a time when he is not likely to be greatly demoralized by the acceptance of what some of our proud old people still consider to be a form of relief, although I do not hold with that view, myself. We are not so likely to demoralize them by offering that form of keep. On the other hand it cancels out a much more serious loss at the other end of the labour market. Two or three years ago we talked about unemployed young persons about the age of twenty-five years. I think to-day we would be justified in placing them between the ages of twenty and twenty-eight years. I say that because 71492-102
I personally know many young persons of twenty-eight years who have had no opportunity of getting permanent employment.
Consequently, while we do not create new jobs by expanding the number of those who have retired upon some form of competence, we do bring in the same number of young people who need work. It is much more important, not only for them individually but for the country as a whole, that they should have work.
I am getting tired of having to go to departments of government or to business employers whom I may happen to know, to plead that a man who has reached the age of sixty-five years may have one more year to make a little more provision, so that there will be one year less in which somebody else will have to support him until he reaches the age of seventy and is able to get his old age pension. Whether or not those people should have been thrifty, whether or not fault is to be found because they are not able to look after themselves in the five years from sixty-five to seventy, the fact remains that the great majority of men, particularly those who live in our cities, are not independent when they reach the age of sixty-five years. I have talked with scores of such men in the last two or three years who have told me that they do not want to hang on to their jobs past sixty-five years of age. They told me they knew of younger men who needed work, but they wanted to know what they could do. Their families could not keep them, and they did not know where they could go or what they could do in the years between sixty-five and seventy.
I am satisfied that now is the time when something should be done about this problem. I do not believe it is an insurmountable problem, but perhaps we may have to sit down to figure out some contributory scheme which would permit of an earlier retirement. The situation for many is hopeless now, but must it go on being hopeless forever? My purpose in rising is to say that if this measure goes to a vote I shall support it in the words of the resolution. I urge the government either to do something now or to give an indication that something will be done. This should not be one of those things which is postponed until the inevitable hour.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	Mr. Speaker, it would be much
more pleasant for me if I could take the side of this question which the hon. members who have spoken have taken. It is much more pleasant to rise in one's place and advocate



Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
the paying of money to people who need it than it is to demonstrate the difficulties attendant upon such a course. I do not think some of the speakers have been fair either to the dominion government, to the provincial governments or to myself as minister in the attitudes they have taken. However, that is part of the responsibility of government and one must accept it. Needless to say, the popular rule in these days is to advocate the paying of money to people. The larger the number of people to whom one can advocate the paying of money, the more likely one is to get sympathetic support. I say again, as I have said before in this house, that no scheme has yet been devised whereby money can be paid by the government to some Canadian people without taking that money in some way or another from all the Canadian people. If I leave out the word "money" and substitute the word "value," perhaps in that statement I may get the support even of my Social Credit friends. However that may be, it is becoming a function of government to an increasing degree, to redistribute wealth. Particularly since the war has this government taken from all to give to some and I am one of those who believe that this tendency will continue.
I consider it to be my duty to bring to the attention of the house the extent to which we do this by way of war pensions, every one of which has been richly earned, to the extent of $50,000,000 or so a year; by way of old age pensions to the extent at the present time of some $30,000,000 a year; by way of relief and so on. We do in fact redistribute five or six hundred million of the national income which comes into the coffers of the treasury. This is redistributed either in the form of payments to individuals, in the form of pensions or relief, or in the form of payments for services which are insisted upon by the community for the community.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Or interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
And interest. By the way, I should tell my hon. friend that interest is the one expenditure which has been decreasing during the last three or four years while all others have been increasing. In spite of an increase in the public debt to the extent of nearly a billion dollars in the last eight years, our interest bill this year is lower than it has been in any year since the war. I think this fact should be stated when we emphasize the payment of interest, which is the wages of money.
With respect to the old age pension system and the principle of old age pensions, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. 
Woodsworth) went into the history of this matter. I sat in the house, as did he and a number of others, when this legislation went through. I am quite prepared to accept the statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to some of the things which were said on that occasion by some of the members. I do not remember them, although I do remember quite distinctly that members on all sides of the house at that time, and indeed prior to that time, were anxiously looking for a way, within the limits of the constitution, by which old age pensions could be commenced in this country. I think that was a general desire on the part of the members of the house at that time, and for several years preceding the actual inauguration of the scheme. Many of us believed that the only type of scheme possible under our constitution would run the risk of not being adopted in some of the provinces. In spite of what our friends in the comer say, there is a real constitutional difficulty in this parliament endeavouring to promulgate something which under the constitution is within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I say again, as I have said before, that there is no better illustration of the long term unwisdom of attempting to evade the constitution by means of agreements between the dominion, on the one hand, and each separate one of the nine provinces, on the other, than the very old age pension scheme we are now discussing. I have had experience in endeavouring to get a degree of provincial unanimity which would make possible improvements in administration in the interests of the old age pensioners, many thousands of whom are within the intent of the law bona fide entitled to old age pensions. At the same time I endeavoured, and I believe the provinces endeavoured, to reach an agreement on regulations which would prevent thousands who were not bona fide entitled to old age pensions under this law from getting them. In spite of the appeals to prejudice made from some quarters of the house to-night, I conceive it to be my duty to endeavour to carry out the law as it was placed upon the statute books of this dominion.
But there are difficulties. One of the real difficulties of abridging the constitution in this matter-because it is really an abridgement by agreement of the plain intent of the constitution that this particular form of activity should be under the provinces and within their sole jurisdiction-is that having entered into agreements with each of the nine provinces, which agreements could not in the very nature of things in connection with experimental legislation foresee all of the

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
thousand and one points which would arise, once the provinces commenced operating the scheme in cooperation with the dominion, minister of finance after minister of finance- not merely myself-had to endeavour time after time to secure that degree of agreement between the nine provinces separately and the dominion which would make it possible to bring this scheme more into harmony with the original intent of the law as we understood the law.
It was not until a little more than a year ago that finally, at a conference, a substantial agreement was reached on many points, not by any means on all the points of difference. The provinces insist that it is their constitutional right to administer this system, that they have an absolute right of veto of any change in the regulations. Please mark that. Each province says:	We have an
agreement with the dominion under the terms of which ten years' notice of termination is required. The province says: We have an agreement with you and that agreement cannot be changed except by mutual consent between the dominion and each individual province. And, Mr. Minister of Justice, they are constitutionally right, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Can hon. members who look solely at the humanitarian aspect of the matter really see the difficulties that are inherent in a situation of that sort?

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
On the other hand we
pay seventy-five per cent of the money. So should we not therefore lay down the conditions under which we pay a major portion of the pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: There would have been no old age pensions had we not agreed to pay fifty per cent. Following through my hon. friend's point to its logical conclusion, what shall we say to the provinces? Shall we say to them: If you will not agree to do precisely as the dominion wishes in this matter, we will do-what? We will give ten years' notice that we are going to terminate the agreement? My hon. friend sees the dilemma.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: But all the provincial governments would be defeated on that score.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I am not discussing the political aspect of it at all, and I am not discussing the political complexion of any provincial government. To be perfectly fair to all of them, in any conference I have been in with the provinces-and they have varied in political complexion from time to time-I have never known the political
aspect to enter into the discussion, and I freely confess that the provinces with their own knowledge of their own conditions are just as sincere and are taking just as sound a humanitarian view of this question as we are sitting in this house.
I am merely trying to make the point that this question of extra-constitutionality, which was never contemplated at confederation, is very difficult to work out in practice. It is for that reason that I have advocated before to-day, and advocate again to-day, that the constitutional responsibility for old age pensions and for unemployment insurance should be federal in character.
I believe, too, very strongly that a public body which has the power to expend money should be responsible for the raising of that money by taxation upon its own constituent body. That I believe to be a vital principle of sound government, and to the extent that we abridge the constitution by agreements in the manner in which we have done in this case, we to that extent at any rate violate that principle and make sound and fair administration more difficult.
Now, having said that, may I say further in defence of the provinces that, in spite of what has been said here, Mr. Speaker, I believe that every province is endeavouring to give fair and sympathetic administration to the Old Age Pensions Act-I believe that honestly-in accordance with what they consider to be their knowledge of their own provincial conditions. We may talk as we like, but twenty dollars a month in Prince Edward Island is worth more to a man or woman than twenty dollars a month in Saskatchewan. All the theorizing in the world will not equalize the cost of living across this dominion, or as between certain urban and certain rural sections of this dominion. That is one of the very reasons why the fathers of confederation divided the jurisdictions as they did, in order that differences in conditions might continuously be dealt with in the light of the smaller area where it is much more likely conditions will be reasonably uniform.
The arguments advanced here to-night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre- who I am sorry is not in his seat at the moment, and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, illustrate one of the great difficulties of the provincial governments-not of the federal government because the federal government has nothing whatever to do with deciding who shall get a pension or how much the individual applicant shall get. The federal government under the law and under the agreement is in the position of agreeing to

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
pay seventy-five per cent of what the province expends, and it may surprise hon. members to know that it was not until 1931, when the amendment to seventy-five per cent was put in the law, that the dominion got the definite power of audit. At the present time we do audit, but every province insists-and the law and the constitution are with them- that it is its right and its power to determine who is qualified under the law and how much under the law that individual shall receive.
May I say that the law never contemplated that a person in receipt of an income of over SI25 a year should get an old age pension. That is written in the law.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: The full pension of $20 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: The full pension of $20 a month, subject to a deduction if the income of the individual reached $125 a year. Let me put it in another way. A person could receive up to $125 a year from other sources without impairing his right to an old age pension.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Of $20 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Of $20 a month, yes. The questions raised as to whether the province has a right to determine whether, when a man and wife live together, they shall receive $15 instead of $20 each, have been the subject of conflict between law officers of the crown in the right of the province and law officers of the crown in the right of the dominion ever since we have had the act, and I assume they will continue to be. I have reams of opinions here from provincial law officers and from our own law officers of the Department of Justice upon the subject. Some of the provinces say that so far as their people are concerned their people really believe that when a man and wife live together they should not get as much as two aged persons living apart. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) may say that the province would be defeated on that. I do not know. That is what they say, and they say it to their own people. They are taking the responsibility. It is impossible for it to be otherwise in that regard.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre objected to prying into the circumstances of these old people who are applicants for pension. Well, Mr. Speaker, I could, on the basis of inquiries that I have addressed to practically all the provinces of this dominion, bring before this house cases by the hundred where these very inquiries have been the only means of revealing that the persons 
applying were not entitled to old age pensions at all within the meaning of the law as it passed this house. They had in fact in a great many instances considerable property and had taken means to distribute it among their families a few years in advance of becoming eligible for old age pensions, and the very families who got it were not willing to keep them. I can tell this house that the provinces of this dominion, if they could reveal it, could show hundreds of instances of undoubted collusion. Their records also show a very great number of cases where the facts only became public after the pensioner had died and property turned up.
How in the world can any provincial administration be sure that an application from John Smith is bona fide and within the law, so far as need is concerned, unless they have provision for investigation and unless they ask all those questions to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre objects? The provincial government is not endowed with second sight. The provincial authorities do not know, when John Smith applies, who he is or what his circumstances are. There is only one method of finding out and that is the method of inquiry. My hon. friend speaks of the insult to these old people in regard to the methods followed of verifying their statements. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie is righteously indignant because in a particular case the provincial government of Manitoba, finding that a woman was working as housekeeper, apparently thought the people for whom she worked ought to pay her wages. My sympathies are wholly with the pensioner in that case. I am of the opinion that when old people work they should be paid the same as young people, and I think the pension authority in any province has a perfect right to insist that anyone getting the services of an old person should pay whatever those services are worth.
With respect to the other matter which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke of, the type of case in which he said children were pressed-harassed was the word I think he used-to provide for their own parents, he referred to the change that had taken place in that regard since he was a boy. There may be a change in the ability of young people to care for their parents; but I do not admit that there is a change in the moral obligation to do so. Neither do I admit that the state should take over a load which an old person's children could assume if they would.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Why pension judges?

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I am not now discussing judges. The Judges Act is not before the house. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will no doubt be willing at any time to give full information with respect to judges; personally I do not have it. I am speaking of a specific matter, old age pensions, and I am trying to stick to it.
I would not advocate for a moment that children who obviously cannot contribute towards the support of their parents should be in any way compelled to do so, but I am one of those who believe that the provincial welfare workers who look into these cases are just as human as the members who have made such a parade of their humanitarianism in the house to-night, and I do believe they give sympathetic consideration to the circumstances of any of the children of pensioners with respect to whom applications come before them. But again I say that this house is not the place to advance complaints against the administration of old age pensions by any province, because of what I have before related as to the basis of the act itself and as to the right of the provinces, claimed insistently, to administer it.
I should give some information again as to what is involved in the resolution. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) has changed his resolution this year. He is not now advocating reduction to a specified age-

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: It is the same as last year's.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
-in the terms of the resolution. He is willing, as he puts it, to agree to any reduction at all as a step in the right direction. I believe he puts five years as the minimum that would satisfy him. I think I know him well enough to be able to say without offence, that I expect that a five-year reduction would satisfy him for one year, and that thereafter, in the light of what he sincerely believes, he would come along year by year in an effort to obtain a further reduction. I appreciate that, and I am not criticizing him for it. So that in the figures I asked to have compiled for me I asked what would be the financial effect of a reduction of the age from seventy to sixty-five.
Before coming to this point, however, perhaps I should indicate that at the present time, in spite of the alleged heartless administration of old age pensions by the various provinces, just about fifty per cent of all the people of Canada who are seventy years and over-just about half of them-are receiving old age pensions. The federal expense in that regard last year was $28,500,000 in round figures, and for the present year the estimates
provide for $30,500,000. Even if we continue the present basis the cost for the next twenty or thirty years will increase very rapidly, though no more generous treatment is accorded. This increase will result partly from the normal growth in population and partly from the fact that in the next twenty-five or thirty years the percentage of our population over seventy to the total population will steadily increase, because our population has been so largely built up in the generation just past by the immigration of adult persons.
Let me give the estimates of our population at future census dates together with the number over seventy years of age, and the cost of old age pensions for them, assuming the present basis, assuming the present proportion, assuming the present rate of payment-and here I must say that these wicked provinces, as alleged to-night, who are so keen to cut down the maximum pension, are in fact to-day paying an average of slightly over $200 per annum to all pensioners. When we bear in mind that the maximum they could pay under the law is $240-if they paid the maximum to every one, that is all they could pay-it certainly does not indicate a heartless chiseling administration on the part of the provinces when the average today is over $200. Assuming then the same proportion as now, the same average payment as now, the cost to the dominion in 1941 would be $46,300,000; in 1951 it would be $62,000,000; in 1961 it would be $82,200,000, and in 1971 it would be $92,800,000.	'

Now, if we lowered the pension age to sixty-five, the immediate additional cost to the dominion alone would be $18,859,000 a year. Or the total immediate cost to the dominion this year, if the age were lowered to sixty, would be $73,900,000.
To the country as a whole the cost would be still greater; for one must remember that the provinces are in this, and this house cannot light-heartedly change this act and assume that every province will accept the financial obligations involved. I know that would not bother the hon. member for Winnipeg North; he would immediately say, "Let the dominion pay the difference whatever it is."
