speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
I think I have said all I want to say about the costs. I leave that part with the house. But I want to say a few words about the growing habit in this house of fouling our own nest as a country. Hardly a discussion of a humanitarian character arises but a number of hon. members state that we are the most backward nation in the world on this and on that. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it. We are not a backward people. In connection with the matter which was discussed just before this resolution, I could have instanced and I wanted to instance that the people of this dominion are not backward in caring for hospitalization and for their sick and their fatherless; they do look after them; they average up as well as any country in the world in that regard. The difficulty is that some hon. members compare what Canada is doing with some country which has either evolved a scheme which enables their national government to do what in our country is a matter for the provinces, or where, as in the case of New Zealand or England, there is a unitary government, not a federal and provincial system of government as we have here. In respect to these matters our people are developing from the bottom up, which is the soundest way.
We had some information this afternoon from the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) indicating how the people themselves are cooperating in providing a measure of health insurance to an increasing degree, which I think is an encouraging sign, and I believe the time will come when we shall deal with the matter from the point of view of dominion assistance to schemes of that sort on the basis of helping self-help. That, indeed, is the basis of the British approach to many of these questions, and is

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
becoming the basis of the approach which is being made in Australia and New Zealand.
With respect to pension schemes, here also we are advancing in Canada every year. An increasing number of Canadian industries are evolving pension schemes. Unfortunately we have not complete details of all of them; we cannot show with chapter and verse the extent to which this movement has grown. In one branch of the government service, operated by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the annuities branch, a remarkable development has taken place within the last two years, through industries utilizing the facilities of the government annuities branch ' in working out pension plans for their industry, in connection with which also I know the Minister of Labour has been mightily criticized from the opposite point of view to that of the criticism we are getting to-night.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people, thank God, are still imbued with sufficient individualism to want to provide for their own security for their old age, as far as they can. There is plenty of evidence of that.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Yes; a good, thick belt to tighten.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: No one is speaking of belt tightening. No, Mr. Speaker; I am referring to those three and a half million Canadians who are trying to provide, in some measure at least, for their own security through the medium of life insurance. I am thinking of those four million Canadians who at this moment have savings deposits in our Canadian banks. They are trying hard to contribute towards the provision of their own security, and the extent-

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: What about the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
My hon. friend can make his speech. Every time I am making a point he just butts in with a boo-boo-boo-boo-boo. If social credit has nothing better than boo-boo-boo-boo-boo, it had better be quiet.
The average Canadian does not want the state to keep him. It is all to his credit that he does not, in my opinion. That does not lessen the obligation of the State to look after its own sick, its own old, its own halt and its own blind. I am not urging that for a moment; but at times, Mr. Speaker, do we not concentrate our attention rather too much on the seven or eight hundred thousand people who are on relief to-night and think rather too little of that great body of our middle-olass represented by those four million of whom I spoke who have some savings and by those three and a half million-of course there would be some overlapping in these two
groups-who are attempting to make provision for their own security by way of life insurance? They are the great burden bearers of this nation, the great middle-class of this country on whom, under any system of taxation, the major burden in proportion to means will rest. I am thinking of them to-night as we speak of those who ought to be maintained by the state, because in the last analysis those who are so maintained are maintained in very large degree by that great middle group of Canadians who are trying to make provision for their own security and who, out of what they do earn or make, are the great body of taxpayers of this dominion.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker., I should like to read what I said in this house on this question last year. Oh, I know I shall be described as reactionary and as orthodox. Thank goodness the ten commandments are orthodox, but they are still pretty good. Speaking for myself, I could repeat to-night every word I said last year, when I made this statement:
In conclusion, I should like to give the house an indication of what I believe our objective should be with regard to old age pensions, and also some idea of the course I think we should pursue in attaining that objective. In the first place, experience in operating this type of social legislation, from the dominion point of view, convinces me that we should look towards a national scheme of old age pensions, nationally administered. I am convinced, in the second place, that the British system of making the lowering of the age limit contingent upon the contributory feature is a sound objective to pursue, and that we should look in that direction. Indeed I am one who believes that there is no limit to what can be worked out in the direction of lowering the age limit, provided we had a national scheme, nationally administered, and provided that the period below seventy years was made definitely contributory.
I think the experience of the British scheme gives us considerable data to work upon in that regard, and I believe that broadly our objective should be, as I have just stated, ultimately to reach a place where we would have a national scheme of old age pensions, nationally administered, and with the contributory feature prominently associated with any ages lower than the age of seventy, which is the present qualifying limit.
Then further on:
Now, as to the course which should be taken to attain them-
That is, the objectives mentioned.
As I indicated at the opening of my remarks, at the present time we are in the position of not having legislative jurisdiction with respect to this matter. There are high constitutional authorities in this house of parliament who take the view that it is doubtful if we have the constitutional authority to pay the seventy-five per cent which we are now paying to the provinces. That view has been expressed on more than one occasion in this house, and

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
while I do not hold with it, at least it gives an indication of the difficulty surrounding the attainment of the national objectives which I have just described.
Therefore we must somehow reach a place where the constitutional authority in the matter is beyond question, where this parliament can set up an old age pensions scheme of a type it deems to be desirable and also have the power to administer. When I say that, it must be remembered that I am not unmindful of the extra cost to the dominion that would be involved or of the fact that if this parliament assumes a burden which the constitution presently places upon the provinces, then this parliament must receive access to fields of taxation, sufficient to enable it to meet the added cost in a national way. If we undertake greater national responsibility, then we must have wider national fields from which to derive the revenues necessary to maintain those national responsibilities and national institutions.
It is well known that in the hearings before the Rowell commission the matter now under discussion was developed I think by every province which appeared before that body. Elaborate and careful studies have been made by economists and welfare workers on behalf of the provinces, and in addition the commission has had its own independent studies made of the question in its relationship to the great question of adjusting the financial relationships between the provinces and the dominion. That is the position in which we are now. In the meantime, under a system which is admittedly faulty because of that bridging of the constitutional difficulty which is involved in the agreement I discussed earlier in my remarks, we are carrying on. I believe we shall reach a point where the provinces will be convinced that the national parliament and the national government-

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: National government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Not in the sense my hon. friend has in mind; perhaps I should say the federal government; "national" is rather a dangerous word to use these days- that the federal parliament and the federal government should have the undoubted right to work out, to enact, to administer and to pay for a national scheme of old age pensions. If I had my way, in introducing such a scheme the remarks I have just made, quoting what I said last year, indicate what I think is the sound course. I am of course, not advancing that as definite government policy. At this stage it would be impossible to introduce such a scheme, but I close with this thought, that in pressing this upon this parliament, hon. members should not forget that the agreements with the provinces in no way estop the provinces from supplementing, out of their own resources, the amount of 
pensions now paid. It is only six or seven years ago that the provinces got fifty per cent from the dominion. When they received an extra twenty-five per cent, did any of them pass it along to the old people in the form of increased pensions? No. The extra contribution was used-as they had a perfect right to use it-in the reduction of their own expenses and their own requirements in the field of taxation.
I have tried to cover the matter as dispassionately as I can, having regard to the fact that I have just as human feelings as any of those who have spoken previously. There is nothing much more difficult than to watch the course of a motion of this kind, or to read letters, such as those which have been read to-night, from an individual who is complaining without having asked the provincial welfare bureau concerned. "What are the facts?"
I have had so much experience of that kind. I have had letters by the hundreds from individuals which I have passed along to the provinces, they having the sole right to deal with the matter. I have asked them if they would be good enough to give me an answer, and I am bound to say in fairness to the provinces that I have yet to find a case where I have not had an answer reasonable at all events, if not fully satisfactory to me.

subtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION OP PENSIONABLE AGE LIMIT FROM SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) upon presenting the resolution to the house. I should like also to pay tribute to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I do not think any hon. member has worked more diligently for social and economic reform.
With regard to the resolution before the house may I say that I am at a loss to know why the government should defend itself. After all, if it is in such an impregnable position it does not require defence. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) tells us that we are just as far ahead as any country in the world. I question that statement, and suggest that Sweden, Great Britain and other nations are far ahead of us in matters of this kind.
The question of money once more arises. We are asked who is going to pay. Well, who always pays? But we will notice this, that when matters of national defence are considered in the house mere dollars and cents do not enter into the debate at all. One cannot compare conditions among the people to-day with those which existed ten or twenty years ago. To-day thousands of young men

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning_
are seeking employment, and the old men are hanging on to their jobs, because those jobs are their only source of security.
When I read the resolution I was reminded of an old friend of mine, an ex-service man of about forty-five or forty-eight years of age. When he looked for work he was told he was too old. I would ask the government if there is any greater social obligation than that of providing security for the aged of our nation. I suppose if anyone were to suggest ways and means by which additional pensions might be financed the Minister of Finance would suggest that we were suggesting pure inflation. How can we pauperize a nation by distributing more goods? I believe that in a debate of this kind, involving the expenditure of money, the government loses sight of the all-important question as to the purpose of an economic system. I say the purpose of an economic system is to produce abundantly and to distribute that which we produce. If it is not that, then there can be no purpose in it.
All the aged ask is the right to live. To-day thousands of them are dispossessed, not only because they are old-although that is one of the greatest contributing factors in competitive society-'but because there is not employment for them. How the government can possibly justify its attitude, wherein it denies the aged the right to security, is more than the average man can understand. All we are asking is that the abundance we can produce may be the measure of security of the aged of our nation-that and nothing more.
For the first time during my experience in the house it appeared to me that the Minister of Finance when speaking lost his equilibrium. He was somewhat annoyed when some members from this corner of the house interfered with his speech. He did not like their butting in. But, many, many times when hon. members in this comer have been speaking, the Minister of Finance and other hon. members opposite have asked questions and made comments. On those occasions there have been very few objections on this side of the house. When the minister loses his equilibrium I take it as final and complete evidence that he is attempting to defend an indefensible position.
Old age pensions are not the responsibility of the provincial governments. It may be that the British North America Act would give that impression, but then we must remember that that act has been the curtain behind which both old-line parties have reneged their obligations to the people of Canada. Will any hon. member sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, say, and have his observation recorded in Hansard, that the age for the old age pension should not be reduced? No, no
hon. member to your right will say that. They are saying, "We have not the money"- but they can find money for national defence and for thousands of other things. But when they are asked for money for the aged, for the youth or for the unemployed, they have no money.
We can provide guns for the west and east coasts; we can build airplanes; we can pass millions of dollars through this house like so many cents for arms and munitions; but when it comes to the real issue of the social security of the people of this nation, then it is a different matter. It has always been the same whether it be the aged, the blind or the unemployed. They do not count; we have no money for them. All we can find money for is to build machine guns, munition factories, and provide other means for the destruction of the state. We have not the intelligence to use our resources for the production of those things which will make life happy and secure and provide a life commensurate with the ability of our people to produce.
What does this resolution ask for? It asks this house to distribute more goods, to give to the aged, to those who are less than seventy years of age, future security. People may boast about democracy, but a parliament that cannot provide security for its aged is bankrupt of progress, bankrupt of everything. It has not an idea. Time and time again sympathy has been expressed in this house for our aged, our unemployed, our ex-service men and our blind, but apparently we have not yet learned that we cannot feed people with sympathy. This matter really requires positive action; it requires the enactment of certain laws to guarantee-what?	Guarantee the
distribution of the goods which we can produce in a scientific age.
When I rose I said that I was not going to speak very long. There is a principle involved here. The Minister of Finance spoke far longer than I shall, and he expressed sympathy in the good old-fashioned Liberal way. But he did not do anything about it. He said he would like to do something, but we have not the money. According to him, the only way we can do anything is to take from those who have little, to give to those who have nothing at least some measure of existence. Are we living in the twentieth century? Can we produce an abundance of things and yet place parliament in a strait-jacket? Can we say, "We should like to give you these things, but we have not the money." What stupidity! I read some of the speeches delivered by Liberal members when they were in opposition, and I was astonished to see the difference between what they say when they are

Old Age Pensions-Mr. Dunning
in opposition and what they say as members of the government. Has not the Liberal party more guts than that? Have they not the courage to fight for the most defenceless people in this nation? If they have not, they should have. I hope they will not be here after 1939, because a government that has lost its courage is no use to a democracy. Democracy demands courage. It demands that we face the facts, not fiction. It demands that we do things, not express sympathy.
Let us get down to facts. The government has said that they are justified in turning down this resolution because the economic system under which we live cannot provide security for these people. The only restriction which the members of the government place upon the providing of this security is the amount of dollars and cents which the chartered banks of Canada can provide. This government does not exist as 245 members; this government is the Minister of Finance. When he cracks the whip everybody jumps. But he is not the whole show. The main show is the Bank of Canada. They are the people who tell the minister what to do, and the government jumps at the crack of the whip. Until this government throws off these shackles of finance; until this government stops saying that nothing can be done every time a suggestion comes from this side of the house, there will be no progress. Until the philosophy of the Minister of Finance is no more; until a new philosophy is predominant there will be no release from the poverty which exists in the country to-day. This resolution gives us an opportunity to bring to the forefront those people of Canada who are so poverty stricken financially, irrespective of the fact that we have so much materially-we are saying we cannot give them more than $20 a month.
